# Mr. Chartist API Bridge: full text

The API overview and every guide, in one file for AI assistants. Generated by scripts/gen-docs-index.mjs; the short index is llms.txt. Links inside the text are relative to the repository.

Operations: 131. Per-endpoint pages: docs/api/README.md.

---

## API overview (from docs/openapi.yaml)

The Bridge runs on your own computer (default `http://127.0.0.1:4300`) and holds your connections to several
brokers and accounts at once. Web apps, webhook alerts (ChartInk, GoCharting, signed scripts), Python and Node scripts, Excel,
Google Sheets and AI assistants all share those connections through this API, so the broker sees one well-behaved
client instead of many.

### Authentication
Every route except `/v1/health`, `/openapi.yaml`, inbound webhooks and the streaming endpoints needs a Bridge API
key: `Authorization: Bearer mcb_<keyId>_<secret>` (or `X-API-Key`). Keys are created with `mc-bridge keys create`
and carry scopes:

| Scope | Allows |
|---|---|
| `read` | market data, instruments, accounts, portfolio, orders list, limits |
| `paper` | `read` + paper orders |
| `live` | `paper` + live orders, only on accounts enabled for live trading in `bridge.config.json`, and only when the request says `"mode": "live"` |
| `admin` | `read` + keys, audit log, kill-switch release, broker sessions; from this computer only |

Keys may also be limited to some accounts. `?key=` in the URL is accepted only on `/xl/*`, and only for
read-only keys created with `--allow-query` (Excel `WEBSERVICE` and AmiBroker cannot send headers).
Streaming endpoints take a short-lived `?token=` from `POST /v1/stream/token`, or an Authorization header.

### Symbols
One canonical, reversible format for every broker:

| Instrument | Example |
|---|---|
| Equity | `NSE:RELIANCE`, `NSE:BAJAJ-AUTO`, `NSE:M&M` |
| Index | `NSE:NIFTY`, `BSE:SENSEX` |
| Future | `NFO:NIFTY-2026-10-27-FUT`, `MCX:CRUDEOIL-2026-11-19-FUT` |
| Option | `NFO:NIFTY-2026-10-27-25000-CE`, `BFO:SENSEX-2026-10-30-82500-PE`, `NFO:VEDL-2026-10-27-292.5-CE` |

`EXCHANGE:UNDERLYING[-YYYY-MM-DD(-FUT | -STRIKE-CE | -STRIKE-PE)]`. Exchange codes are NSE and BSE (cash and
indices), NFO and BFO (equity derivatives), MCX and CDS. The ISO expiry removes the ambiguity of exchange trading
symbols (weekly codes, DDMMMYY vs YYMDD), the suffix is parsed from the right so hyphens in names are safe, and no
lookup is needed to read it. Inputs are lenient (case, `NSE:` for derivatives, chart tickers such as
`NSE:NIFTY1!`, compact symbols with an exchange); responses always use the canonical form. Convert with
`/v1/symbols/convert`.

### Responses, freshness and errors
JSON responses under `/v1` are `{ "data": ..., "meta": { "requestId": ..., ... } }`. Every market-data item carries
`freshness` (`source`: stream, cache, broker, paper, backup or plugin; `asOf`; `ageMs`; `stale`; which account served
it; and how current the data is: `class` realtime, delayed or eod, `delaySec`, `official`, `confidence`, `flags`), so you
always know how old a number is and where it came from. Errors are RFC 9457 `application/problem+json` with a stable `code` and a
`retryable` flag. Times are ISO-8601 with the IST offset (`+05:30`) unless an endpoint says otherwise; candle times
are epoch seconds. List endpoints are paginated with `limit` and an opaque `cursor` (`meta.nextCursor`).

### Data sources
Real-time data and option chains come from your own broker accounts. Optional free sources and plugins (see
`/v1/sources`) add history, cross-checks and graceful fallback; their answers are labelled `delayed` or `eod`, never
blended into a real-time answer, and orders, risk checks, paper fills and alerts (`purpose` = `order`, `risk`, `paper`,
`alert`) accept only real-time data. Guide: docs/guides/sources.md. Developers: docs/source-contract.md.

### Rate limits
The Bridge never exceeds a broker's documented limit. It serves from live streams first, then a short freshness
cache, then batches and coalesces broker calls, with orders always ahead of reads. Your own per-key limit is shown in
`RateLimit` and `RateLimit-Policy` headers (IETF draft; syntax may change). On 429, wait `Retry-After` seconds. A
refusal also says which limit tripped: `scope` (`client`, `upstream`, `queue`, `consumer-cap`), `retryAfterMs` and
`limit` in the problem body; clients should read those, not `detail`. Each key has its own quota and fair-queue
weight (`/v1/quotas`), and `GET /v1/limits?explain=1` shows the shared pools and each consumer's share.

### Orders and safety
Paper mode is the default. A live order needs: `safety.liveTrading` and the account's `live.enabled` in the config
file, a `live` key, the request source allowed for that account, `"mode": "live"` in the request, and every safety
check (kill switch, order-rate cap default 5/s per account, daily order and loss limits, value and lot caps, price
band, market-order protection). Send an `Idempotency-Key` with every order write; a retry with the same key returns
the first result. A write that times out returns `OUTCOME_UNKNOWN`: check the order book before sending it again.

### Demo mode
`mc-bridge start --demo` serves generated sample data from a demo adapter with no broker connected and live
trading off. Operations marked `x-demo-only: true` (under `/v1/demo/`) exist only in demo mode; a Bridge with real
accounts answers them with 404.

Personal use only: broker data terms generally forbid passing market data to other people.

---

<!-- docs/guides/quickstart.md -->

# Quickstart: five minutes to a first answer

This guide takes you from a fresh clone to a price, a paper order, a list of data sources and a live stream. It runs in
**demo mode**, so you need no broker account and no money. Every command and output below was run on a clean checkout;
long output is trimmed with `...` and the keys and one-time codes are shortened.

**Demo caveat.** In demo mode the prices are *sample data generated on your computer*, not market data. The Bridge says
so everywhere: `GET /v1/health` has `"demo": true`, every answer's `meta` carries a `dataNotice`, and the dashboard shows
a Demo badge. Orders go to a paper account. Because the demo "broker" is built in, an answer labelled
`"source": "broker"` here is still sample data; check `demo` before you trust a number.

You need Node.js 22.12 or newer (`node -v`) and git. The examples use the default address `http://127.0.0.1:4300`.

## 1. Get the code and start the Bridge

```bash
git clone https://github.com/MrChartist/api-bridge-v2.git
cd api-bridge-v2
npm ci
npm run dev
```

`npm run dev` is `mc-bridge start --demo --open`. It prints a banner, the data folder and a sign-in link for the
dashboard, and keeps running (stop it with Ctrl+C):

```text
> @mrchartist/api-bridge-v2@2.0.0 dev
> node bin/mc-bridge.mjs start --demo --open

  ************************************************************
  *  DEMO MODE: sample data, not live market data.           *
  *  No broker is connected. Orders are paper only.          *
  ************************************************************

Mr. Chartist API Bridge listening on http://127.0.0.1:4300
Data folder: /home/you/.mc-bridge/data
Dashboard (this computer only): http://127.0.0.1:4300/dashboard
No API keys yet. Open the dashboard signed in with: npm run bridge -- open   (or make one: npm run bridge -- keys create --label me --scope admin,paper)
Market data: demo (sample prices generated on this computer).
Open this link in your browser to see the dashboard, already signed in. It works once and expires in 10 minutes:
  http://127.0.0.1:4300/dashboard#signin=<one-time code>
Press Ctrl+C to stop.
```

(Your data folder will differ: `~/.mc-bridge` on Mac and Linux, `%APPDATA%\MrChartist\Bridge` on Windows.) The browser
opens the dashboard by itself when it can; if it does not, use the link above. Leave this terminal running.

## 2. Make an API key

Open a **second terminal** in the same folder. Each tool gets its own key with only the access it needs. This one can
read and place paper orders:

```bash
npm run bridge -- keys create --label quickstart --scope read,paper
```

```text
Created key bizshnjiv3 (read, paper). Copy it now; it will not be shown again:

  mcb_bizshnjiv3_<the rest of the key>
```

(The CLI also prints a note saying which folder the keys live in.) Keep the key in an environment variable. The Bridge
stores only a fingerprint, so a lost key cannot be shown again: revoke it and make a new one.

```bash
export MCB_API_KEY=mcb_bizshnjiv3_...      # paste your own key
```

On Windows PowerShell: `$env:MCB_API_KEY = "mcb_..."`.

## 3. Ask for health and a price

The health check needs no key:

```bash
curl -s http://127.0.0.1:4300/v1/health
```

```json
{
  "status": "ok",
  "version": "2.0.0",
  "demo": true,
  "dataNotice": "Demo data: sample prices generated on this computer. Not live market data; no broker is connected."
}
```

(The real answer also lists each internal service as `ready`; trimmed here.) Now a price, with your key:

```bash
curl -s "http://127.0.0.1:4300/v1/ltp?symbols=NSE:RELIANCE,NSE:NIFTY" -H "Authorization: Bearer $MCB_API_KEY"
```

```json
{"data":[
  {"symbol":"NSE:RELIANCE","ltp":1461.5,"freshness":{"source":"broker","class":"realtime","official":true,"stale":false, "...": "..."}},
  {"symbol":"NSE:NIFTY","ltp":24882.2,"freshness":{"source":"broker","class":"realtime","official":true,"stale":false, "...": "..."}}
],"errors":[],"meta":{"requestId":"req_...","demo":true,"dataNotice":"Demo data: ..."}}
```

(Reformatted and trimmed; your numbers will differ because demo prices move.) The `freshness` block is how the Bridge is
honest about data: it says where the value came from, whether it is real-time, and how old it is. Symbols are
`EXCHANGE:SYMBOL`.

## 4. Place a paper order

Every order carries an `Idempotency-Key` (8 to 255 letters, digits or `_ . : -`) so a retry can never place it twice.
`demo-paper` is the paper account that demo mode creates.

```bash
curl -s -X POST http://127.0.0.1:4300/v1/orders \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $MCB_API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "Idempotency-Key: quickstart-1" \
  -d '{"account":"demo-paper","symbol":"NSE:RELIANCE","side":"BUY","quantity":1,"product":"CNC","orderType":"MARKET"}'
```

```json
{
  "orderId": "PAPER-20261109-000001",
  "mode": "paper",
  "symbol": "NSE:RELIANCE",
  "side": "BUY",
  "quantity": 1,
  "status": "filled",
  "avgPrice": 1461.7
}
```

(This is the `data` part of the answer, trimmed to the main fields.) `"mode": "paper"` is on every order result. The order
now shows on the dashboard's Orders page too.

Live trading is off, and the Bridge shows what that means. The same call with `"mode": "live"` is refused:

```bash
curl -s -X POST http://127.0.0.1:4300/v1/orders \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $MCB_API_KEY" -H "Content-Type: application/json" -H "Idempotency-Key: quickstart-live-1" \
  -d '{"account":"demo-paper","symbol":"NSE:RELIANCE","side":"BUY","quantity":1,"product":"CNC","orderType":"MARKET","mode":"live"}'
```

```json
{"status":403,"code":"PAPER_ONLY","detail":"demo-paper is a paper account; it cannot place live orders."}
```

(Trimmed to those fields.) Going live takes several separate opt-ins, described in [safety.md](safety.md). Nothing in
this guide can turn it on.

## 5. See where data comes from

```bash
curl -s http://127.0.0.1:4300/v1/sources -H "Authorization: Bearer $MCB_API_KEY"
```

Trimmed to one line per source:

```json
{"id":"demo","kind":"broker","enabled":true,"class":"realtime","delaySec":0,"official":true}
{"id":"demo-delayed","kind":"free","enabled":false,"class":"delayed","delaySec":900,"official":false}
{"id":"demo-eod","kind":"free","enabled":false,"class":"eod","delaySec":null,"official":true}
```

In demo mode the list holds the demo broker and two sample sources, so you can see how a delayed (`delaySec` 900, not
official) and an end-of-day source look. With real accounts, your brokers give real-time data and the free sources
(off until you turn them on) give delayed or end-of-day data. Read [sources.md](sources.md) before turning one on. The
dashboard's Sources page shows the same information, plus how much request room is left.

## 6. Watch a live stream

A WebSocket stream needs a single-use token so your key never goes into a URL. Save this as `stream.mjs` in the
repository folder (the `ws` package is already installed there by `npm ci`):

```js
import WebSocket from "ws";

const BASE = process.env.MCB_URL ?? "http://127.0.0.1:4300";
const KEY = process.env.MCB_API_KEY;

// A stream token is single use and lasts 60 seconds, so the key never appears in a URL.
const res = await fetch(`${BASE}/v1/stream/token`, { method: "POST", headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${KEY}` } });
const { data } = await res.json();

const ws = new WebSocket(`${BASE.replace("http", "ws")}/v1/stream?token=${encodeURIComponent(data.token)}`);
let ticks = 0;
ws.on("open", () => ws.send(JSON.stringify({ op: "subscribe", symbols: ["NSE:RELIANCE"], mode: "ltp", id: "s1" })));
ws.on("message", (raw) => {
  const m = JSON.parse(raw);
  console.log(m.type, m.symbol ?? "", m.ltp ?? "");
  if (m.type === "tick" && ++ticks === 3) ws.close();
});
```

```bash
node stream.mjs
```

```text
heartbeat  
status  
snapshot  
tick NSE:RELIANCE 1461.7
tick NSE:RELIANCE 1461.7
tick NSE:RELIANCE 1461.7
```

The `heartbeat`, `status` and `snapshot` messages come first; then a `tick` for every price change. (Demo prices change
slowly, so ticks can repeat a value.) The message formats are in [streaming.md](streaming.md). Node 22 also has a
built-in `WebSocket`, so outside this folder you do not need `ws`.

## 7. Stop and clean up

Press Ctrl+C in the first terminal. Your keys and paper orders stay in the data folder. To start over, see
[How do I reset?](faq.md#how-do-i-reset) in the FAQ.

## Troubleshooting

### Port already in use

Starting the Bridge fails at once:

```text
Error: Port 4300 is already in use by another program (not this Bridge). Close that program, or choose another port under "server" in bridge.config.json (for example "port": 4301).
```

Close the other program, or use another port for this run with an environment variable:

```bash
MCB_PORT=4301 npm run dev
```

Every later command that talks to the Bridge (`npm run bridge -- open`, `doctor`, `curl`) must use the same port. If you
forget, `npm run bridge -- open` answers `The Bridge is not running at http://127.0.0.1:4300`. To keep the port, put
`"server": { "port": 4301 }` in `bridge.config.json`.

If a Bridge is already running, starting a second one says so instead:

```text
The Bridge is already running at http://127.0.0.1:4300. To open its dashboard, run: mc-bridge open
```

If that Bridge keeps its files in another folder, you get `A Bridge is running at ..., but it keeps its files in another
folder than ...`: run the command from the folder you started it in, or stop it and start it again.

### Node version

The Bridge needs Node.js 22.12 or newer. Check with `node -v`. `npm run doctor` prints a `Node.js <version>` line and
marks it as failed with "(22 or newer is required)" on an older version. Install a current Node.js (or use the
[one-step installer](install.md), which brings its own) and run `npm ci` again.

### The key is not accepted (401)

A 401 has a `detail` that tells you which of three things is wrong:

| `detail` | Cause and fix |
|---|---|
| `Send your Bridge API key as 'Authorization: Bearer <key>'.` | No key, or the header is not in the `Authorization: Bearer <key>` form (a bare key, or `X-API-Key`, is not accepted). The shell variable may also be empty: run `echo $MCB_API_KEY`. |
| `This API key is not valid, has expired or was revoked.` | The key is mistyped or cut off (a key looks like `mcb_<id>_<secret>` and is shown only once), was revoked, or has expired. Make a new one. |
| the same text, but the key is fresh | The key was made for a *different data folder* than the running Bridge uses (for example the CLI ran with another `MCB_HOME` or config file). The CLI prints "keys live in `<folder>`" when it creates a key; compare that with the "Data folder" line the Bridge printed at start. Run `keys create` from the same folder, with the same `MCB_HOME` or `--config`. |

A key that is valid but lacks the access gets a 403 instead. A key made with `--scope read` that places an order is
answered `SCOPE_REQUIRED: This API key needs the "paper" scope.` Make a key with the scope it needs. A missing or too short `Idempotency-Key` is a 400 `VALIDATION_FAILED` naming the
header.

### The dashboard asks you to sign in

You see "Sign in with an admin key". The dashboard keeps its session in the browser *tab* and forgets it when the tab is
closed, and the sign-in link printed at start works **once** and expires after 10 minutes. Get a fresh link:

```bash
npm run bridge -- open
```

```text
Open this link in your browser to see the dashboard, already signed in. It works once and expires in 10 minutes:
  http://127.0.0.1:4300/dashboard#signin=<one-time code>
```

(Or paste an admin key into the sign-in box: `npm run bridge -- keys create --label me --scope admin,paper`.) The dashboard
works only on the computer running the Bridge. Use the same port and data folder as the running Bridge, as above.

### Requests are refused with 429

A 429 means a limit said no, and the body says whose. This one is from a key whose quota was lowered to one request a
second (`PUT /v1/quotas/<keyId>` with `{"perSecond":1,"burst":2}`; the third request in a second is refused):

```text
HTTP/1.1 429 Too Many Requests
Retry-After: 1
Content-Type: application/problem+json
```

```json
{"title":"Too many requests from this API key","status":429,"detail":"This API key is sending more than 1 requests a second (burst 2). Try again in 944 ms.","code":"RATE_LIMITED","retryable":true,"retryAfterMs":944,"scope":"client","limit":{"name":"perSecond","remaining":0,"resetMs":944}}
```

Read these fields, not the text:

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `scope` | Whose limit: `client` (this API key's own rate, daily cap or requests in flight), `consumer-cap` (this key already has too many requests waiting), `queue` (the shared queue for that account is full) or `upstream` (the broker's own budget cannot serve you in time) |
| `retryAfterMs` | How long to wait before trying again; `Retry-After` is the same in whole seconds |
| `limit` | The budget that refused: its `name`, what `remaining` and when it resets (`resetMs`) |

For `client` and `consumer-cap`, slow the tool down or raise that key's quota (dashboard: Sources, Quotas). For
`queue` and `upstream`, wait `retryAfterMs`, or read from the stream or cache instead of polling. More in
[rate-limits.md](rate-limits.md).

<!-- docs/guides/faq.md -->

# FAQ

Short answers, each pointing at the guide that has the details.

## Is it free?

The Bridge is free, open-source software under the [MIT License](../../LICENSE). There is no hosted service and no account
with us: it runs on your computer. What can cost money is outside the Bridge. Some brokers charge for their API or for
live market data, and some data vendors have paid plans. For example, [BROKERS.md](../BROKERS.md#limits-live-feed-and-data-plans)
lists brokers whose live quotes need a paid plan, and the Twelve Data and Alpha Vantage sources in
[sources.md](sources.md) need your own vendor key (and a paid plan for Indian data on Twelve Data). Check your broker's
current pricing.

## Is my broker supported?

41 brokers are supported; the list, with how each logs in and what it can do, is in [BROKERS.md](../BROKERS.md) and on the
dashboard's Accounts page. Only **Dhan** has been verified end to end with a live account. The other 40 are **beta**:
written from the broker's official documentation and tested against recorded sample responses. Live order mapping exists
only for Dhan (verified) and for Zerodha and Upstox (beta, with a warning on every live order); for every other broker the
Bridge answers a live order with a "use paper mode" error. Reading data and paper trading work wherever the adapter says
they do.

If your broker is not on the list, open the "New broker request" issue form (see [CONTRIBUTING.md](../../CONTRIBUTING.md)).
Adapters are written only from a broker's official documentation.

## Why is pooling off?

Pooling means using the request budgets of several of *your own* accounts to serve market-data reads, so busy tools get
more room. No broker's published terms clearly allow it, and none clearly forbids it; a few say things that could matter.
So the Bridge leaves it off until you accept a notice that names the risk, and then it only ever pools accounts of one
holder, only for reads, and never moves an order. Orders always go through the account they belong to. The details and
the per-broker findings are in [rate-limits.md](rate-limits.md#spreading-reads-across-your-own-accounts-pooling). You are
responsible for following your brokers' terms; get a legal read if you are unsure.

## Why can't I get real-time data from Yahoo?

Because Yahoo does not offer it, and the Bridge does not pretend it does. Yahoo Finance is an unofficial, delayed source
(about 15 minutes), and its terms restrict automated access. It is off by default; you turn it on by reading a notice, and
every answer from it is labelled `"class": "delayed"` and `"official": false`. It is meant for charts, history and your own
cross-checks. Real-time Indian market data is licensed by the exchanges, and no free official source of it exists that you
may redistribute, so real-time prices come from your own broker account. Orders, risk checks, paper fills and alerts accept
only real-time data from a broker; the Bridge refuses to use a delayed or end-of-day source for them. See
[sources.md](sources.md).

## Is paper trading safe?

For your money, yes: a paper order is simulated locally and never reaches a broker. Every order is paper unless a request
passes every live-trading opt-in ([safety.md](safety.md)), and a live request that misses one is refused, not quietly
downgraded. But paper results are not a forecast of live results. The simulator fills market orders at the opposite best
price or the last price plus slippage, has no queue position, partial fills or market impact, and approximates margin
rather than computing a broker's own. In demo mode the prices are sample data. Do not size a real strategy from paper
profits alone.

## Where is my data stored?

On your computer, in the Bridge's data folder, which is printed when the Bridge starts (`Data folder: ...`). By default it
is `~/.mc-bridge/data` on Mac and Linux and `%APPDATA%\MrChartist\Bridge\data` on Windows; `MCB_HOME` or `dataDir` in
`bridge.config.json` change it. In it you will find the API key list (fingerprints, not the keys), the encrypted store of broker
credentials and source keys (once you add any), the audit log, orders and paper accounts, safety counters and the
instrument cache. The Bridge listens on `127.0.0.1`, so other computers cannot reach it. The Bridge has no telemetry. It talks to your brokers and to any free
or key-based data source you turn on, and to the IP-lookup address only if you turn on that optional readiness check
([deployment.md](deployment.md)). `npm run doctor` also warns when the
encryption master key sits in the data folder next to the secrets, because a backup of the folder then carries both.

## How do I reset?

- **Paper account only:** on the dashboard's Accounts page, press Reset funds, or call
  `POST /v1/paper/accounts/{id}/reset` (a key with the `paper` scope; optional `{"startingCapital": 500000}`). It clears
  paper orders and positions. `POST /v1/paper/accounts/{id}/reset/undo` puts the old book back for 2 minutes, if no order
  has been placed since.
- **A key:** revoke it on the API page or with `npm run bridge -- keys revoke <keyId>`, and make a new one.
- **Everything, starting fresh:** stop the Bridge (Ctrl+C), then move or delete the data folder. That removes keys, paper
  state, the audit log and any stored broker credentials. To try the Bridge without touching your real folder, point it at an
  empty one: `MCB_HOME=$(mktemp -d) npm run dev`. If you installed with the one-line installer, `--purge` removes the data
  too ([install.md](install.md)).

## More questions

[Quickstart troubleshooting](quickstart.md#troubleshooting) covers a port in use, a key that is not accepted, the dashboard
asking you to sign in and 429 refusals. For anything else, search the
[issues](https://github.com/MrChartist/api-bridge-v2/issues) or open one.

---

<!-- docs/guides/install.md -->

# Installing the Bridge

You do not need to know anything about programming. Pick **one** way below. Each takes a few minutes and needs no
admin password. You never have to install Node.js yourself, and you never have to copy a key: the dashboard opens in
your browser already signed in.

Everything stays on your computer. Orders are **paper** (practice, with virtual money) until you switch real trading on
yourself in the settings file.

| Your computer | Easiest way |
|---|---|
| Windows 10 or 11 | [Setup.exe](#windows-setupexe) (double-click) or [one line in PowerShell](#windows-one-line) |
| Mac | [One line in Terminal](#mac-and-linux-one-line) (no security prompts) or [the ready-to-run download](#ready-to-run-download) |
| Linux | [One line in a terminal](#mac-and-linux-one-line) or [the ready-to-run download](#ready-to-run-download) |
| Android phone or tablet | [Termux and one line](#android-termux) |

---

## Windows: Setup.exe

1. Open the [latest release](https://github.com/MrChartist/api-bridge-v2/releases/latest) and download
   **`Mr-Chartist-Bridge-Setup-….exe`**.
2. Double-click it. If Windows says *"Windows protected your PC"*, click **More info**, then **Run anyway** (the file
   is not signed yet; this happens only once).
3. A small window shows the progress, then the Bridge starts and your browser opens the dashboard, already signed in.

That is all: no admin password, nothing else to install (Node.js is inside the .exe). Next time, open
**Mr Chartist Bridge** from the Start menu or the Desktop. To remove it: **Settings → Apps → Installed apps →
Mr. Chartist API Bridge → Uninstall** (your settings and data are kept). Running a newer Setup.exe updates it.

---

## Ready-to-run download

Everything the Bridge needs is inside the ZIP, including its own copy of Node.js, so it works even without internet
while installing.

1. Open the [latest release](https://github.com/MrChartist/api-bridge-v2/releases/latest) and download the file for your
   computer:
   - Windows: `mr-chartist-bridge-…-windows-x64.zip`
   - Mac with Apple chip (M1, M2, M3, M4…): `…-macos-arm64.zip`; older Intel Mac: `…-macos-x64.zip`
     (Apple menu → About This Mac shows which)
   - Linux PC: `…-linux-x64.zip`; Raspberry Pi and other ARM boards: `…-linux-arm64.zip`
2. Unzip it (double-click the ZIP; on Windows choose **Extract all**). You get a folder called **Mr Chartist Bridge**.
   Put it anywhere you like, for example in Documents.
3. Open the folder and double-click the start file:
   - Windows: **`start-windows.bat`**. If Windows says *"Windows protected your PC"*, click **More info**, then
     **Run anyway**. This happens only the first time.
   - Mac: **`start-mac.command`**. The first time, macOS blocks it because it was downloaded from the internet:
     - macOS 15 (Sequoia) or newer: open **System Settings → Privacy & Security**, scroll down and click
       **Open Anyway**, then confirm.
     - macOS 14 or older: right-click the file, choose **Open**, then **Open** again.
   - Linux: **`start-linux.sh`** (or open a terminal in the folder and type `sh start-linux.sh`).
4. A small window opens and your browser shows the dashboard, already signed in. **Keep the small window open** while
   you use the Bridge. To stop the Bridge, close that window.

Next time, double-click the same start file again.

---

## Mac and Linux: one line

1. Open **Terminal** (Mac: press <kbd>⌘ Space</kbd>, type *Terminal*, press Enter; Linux: your applications menu).
2. Copy this line, paste it into Terminal and press Enter:

   ```sh
   curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/MrChartist/api-bridge-v2/main/install.sh | sh
   ```

3. Wait a minute or two. It downloads the Bridge (and its own Node.js if your computer does not have Node.js 22),
   sets it up and opens the dashboard, already signed in.

Next time, start it like any app:

- **Mac:** open **Mr Chartist Bridge** from Spotlight (<kbd>⌘ Space</kbd>, type *Mr Chartist*) or Launchpad.
- **Linux:** **Mr Chartist Bridge** in your applications menu, or the icon on your Desktop.

Want to try it with sample prices first, without any broker? Use:

```sh
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/MrChartist/api-bridge-v2/main/install.sh | sh -s -- --demo
```

---

## Windows: one line

1. Click **Start**, type **PowerShell** and open **Windows PowerShell** (no need for "Run as administrator").
2. Copy this line, paste it (right-click pastes) and press Enter:

   ```powershell
   irm https://raw.githubusercontent.com/MrChartist/api-bridge-v2/main/install.ps1 | iex
   ```

3. Wait a minute or two. It downloads the Bridge (and its own Node.js if needed), sets it up, adds
   **Mr Chartist Bridge** to your Start menu and Desktop, and opens the dashboard, already signed in.

Next time, start it from the **Mr Chartist Bridge** shortcut on your Desktop or in the Start menu.

## Android (Termux)

The Bridge runs on an Android phone or tablet inside **Termux**, a free Linux terminal app. Its API and dashboard
are then on the phone itself, at `http://127.0.0.1:4300`.

1. Install **Termux** from [F-Droid](https://f-droid.org/packages/com.termux/) (the Play Store version is outdated).
   Optional: also install **Termux:Widget** from F-Droid for a home-screen shortcut.
2. Open Termux, paste this line and press Enter:

   ```sh
   pkg install -y curl && curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/MrChartist/api-bridge-v2/main/install.sh | sh
   ```

   It installs Node.js with Termux's own package manager (no root), sets up paper trading and opens the dashboard in
   your browser, already signed in.
3. Keep Termux open while you use the Bridge. Android may pause apps in the background: the Bridge asks for a Termux
   wake lock while it runs, and you can also set Termux to **Unrestricted** under Android Settings → Apps → Termux →
   Battery.

Next time, tap the **Mr Chartist Bridge** widget, or type `mc-bridge start --open` in Termux. Other devices on your
Wi-Fi cannot reach it unless you deliberately allow that in `bridge.config.json`; that is on purpose.

## After installing

- **Lost the dashboard tab?** Start the Bridge again from its shortcut (or double-click the start file). If it is
  already running, that simply opens the dashboard again, signed in.
- **Connect your broker:** on the dashboard, open **Accounts**.
- **Try everything with sample prices:** see [demo mode](quickstart.md).
- **Update to a new version:** run the same one line again (your settings and data are kept), or download the new ZIP
  and copy your `bridge.config.json` and `data` folder into the new folder.

## Uninstalling

| How you installed | How to remove it |
|---|---|
| One line on Mac or Linux | `curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/MrChartist/api-bridge-v2/main/install.sh \| sh -s -- --uninstall` (your settings and data stay in `~/.mc-bridge`; add `--purge` to delete them too) |
| One line on Windows | `$env:MCB_UNINSTALL = "1"; irm https://raw.githubusercontent.com/MrChartist/api-bridge-v2/main/install.ps1 \| iex` (your settings and data stay in `%APPDATA%\MrChartist\Bridge`) |
| Setup.exe on Windows | **Settings → Apps → Installed apps → Mr. Chartist API Bridge → Uninstall** (your settings and data stay in `%APPDATA%\MrChartist\Bridge`) |
| Ready-to-run download | Delete the **Mr Chartist Bridge** folder. |
| Android (Termux) | In Termux: `curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/MrChartist/api-bridge-v2/main/install.sh \| sh -s -- --uninstall` |

## If something goes wrong

| What you see | What to do |
|---|---|
| "Could not download …" | Check your internet connection and run it again. Office networks sometimes block downloads; try at home. |
| The browser does not open | Copy the link printed in the small window into your browser. It works once, for 10 minutes; start again for a new one. |
| "Port 4300 is already in use by another program" | Another program uses the Bridge's port. Close it, or change `server.port` in `bridge.config.json`. |
| "This sign-in link has expired or was already used" | Start the Bridge again from its shortcut; it opens a fresh link. |
| Anything else | Run `mc-bridge doctor` (or, in the download folder, the start file again) and [open an issue](https://github.com/MrChartist/api-bridge-v2/issues) with what it prints. Never paste your keys. |

For developers: `git clone`, `npm ci`, `npm run dev`; see the [quickstart](quickstart.md) and [CONTRIBUTING.md](../../CONTRIBUTING.md).
Docker: see the [README](../../README.md#docker).

<!-- docs/guides/accounts.md -->

# Brokers and multiple accounts

The Bridge holds connections to several brokers and several accounts at once. Each account has its own session, its
own rate-limit budget and its own credentials; one account's credentials are never used for another account's calls.

## 1. Declare accounts in `bridge.config.json`

The easiest way: on the dashboard, open **Accounts** and press **Add a broker**. The Bridge saves the account to the
config file it loaded (or creates the per-user `bridge.config.json` when it started without one) and uses it at once,
no restart. Accounts added this way are paper only; turning live trading on stays an edit of the file. **Remove**
takes an account out again (not one with live trading set up, and not your last paper account). Over the API:
`POST /v1/accounts` with `{ "broker": "dhan" }` (optional `id` and `label`) and `DELETE /v1/accounts/{id}`, both
admin, this computer only, with an admin key that may use every account.

Or edit the file yourself:

```json
{
  "accounts": [
    { "id": "dhan-main",      "broker": "dhan",    "label": "Dhan (main)" },
    { "id": "zerodha-main",   "broker": "zerodha", "label": "Zerodha (main)" },
    { "id": "zerodha-spouse", "broker": "zerodha", "label": "Zerodha (spouse)", "enabled": true },
    { "id": "paper",          "broker": "paper",   "label": "Practice account" }
  ]
}
```

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `id` | Your name for the account: 2-32 lowercase letters, digits or hyphens. Used everywhere (`account=` in queries, `"account"` in orders). |
| `broker` | Adapter id from [BROKERS.md](../BROKERS.md), or `paper`. |
| `label` | Shown on the dashboard and in API responses. |
| `enabled` | `false` keeps the account in the file but out of use. |
| `holder` | Whose account it is (`self`, `spouse` ...; never a PAN). Pooling only ever joins accounts of one holder. |
| `marketData.pooling` | Opt in to letting this account serve other unpinned reads (see [rate-limits.md](rate-limits.md)). Off by default. Pooling also needs your consent, below. |
| `marketData.poolingWhenTermsUnknown` | Also pool when the broker's terms on this are not confirmed (every broker today). Your decision; off by default. |
| `live` | `{ "enabled": false, "allowedSources": ["rest"], "registeredIp": "..." }`; see [safety.md](safety.md). Off by default. |
| `limits` | Per-account safety limits that may only be stricter than the global `safety` section. |

`npx mc-bridge accounts list` shows what the Bridge read. `npx mc-bridge doctor` checks the file.

## 2. Log in

Credentials never go in the config file. They go to the encrypted SecretStore (`data/secrets.enc`, AES-256-GCM)
through `POST /v1/accounts/{id}/session`, which answers only on this computer and needs an admin key.
The dashboard's **Log in** button (Accounts page) shows the fields your broker needs and calls it for you;
`mc-bridge accounts connect <accountId>` does the same in a terminal.

`GET /v1/brokers` lists every broker with its `authKind` and the fields it needs (`credentialFields`). There are four
kinds of login:

| Kind | What you send | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| `apiKeyToken` | `values` with the broker's token fields | Dhan (`clientId`, `accessToken`), Groww, Samco |
| `oauthRedirect` | `values` with the API key, secret and the access token from the broker's login page | Zerodha, Upstox, Fyers |
| `requestTokenExchange` | `values` with the request code from the broker's login page; the Bridge exchanges it | Shoonya, Flattrade, Alice Blue |
| `sessionLogin` | `values` (API key, client id) plus `secrets` (PIN or password and the **current** TOTP code) | Angel One, Kotak, Motilal Oswal |

Example for Angel One (`GET /v1/brokers` shows each broker's exact `loginFields`):

```bash
curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:4300/v1/accounts/angel-main/session \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $MCB_ADMIN_KEY" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"values": {"apiKey": "...", "clientId": "A123"}, "secrets": {"password": "<PIN>", "totpCode": "123456"}}'
```

```bash
curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:4300/v1/accounts/dhan-main/session \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $MCB_ADMIN_KEY" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"values": {"clientId": "1100000000", "accessToken": "eyJ..."}}'
```

For `sessionLogin` brokers the password, PIN and TOTP code are passed to the broker's login call once and then
dropped. They are never stored, logged, cached or used as a cache key. Only the session token the broker returns is
kept, encrypted.

Check and test:

```bash
curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $MCB_ADMIN_KEY" http://127.0.0.1:4300/v1/accounts
curl -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer $MCB_ADMIN_KEY" http://127.0.0.1:4300/v1/accounts/dhan-main/test
curl -X DELETE -H "Authorization: Bearer $MCB_ADMIN_KEY" http://127.0.0.1:4300/v1/accounts/dhan-main/session   # log out
```

## 3. Sessions

States: `missing` → `connected` → `expired` or `error`. Most brokers end API sessions early every morning (SEBI
requires a daily logout). When a broker rejects a session, the Bridge marks the account `expired` straight away, and
reads that need it answer `SESSION_EXPIRED` with a plain message. Log in again; nothing else changes. The Bridge never
stores TOTP secrets and never automates 2FA.

If you change credentials with another tool while the Bridge runs, it notices the change to `data/secrets.enc` and
reloads.

## 4. Family accounts

SEBI's retail algo rules allow use by you, your spouse, dependent children and dependent parents. Add each as its
own account. Limit API keys to the accounts a tool needs:

```bash
npx mc-bridge keys create --label spouse-sheet --scope read --accounts zerodha-spouse --expires 30d
```

Do not add anyone else's accounts: the Bridge is personal software, not a service for other people.

## 5. Choosing an account per request

- `account=<id>` (query) or `"account": "<id>"` (order body) pins the request to that account.
- Without it, market-data reads use the primary account (the first enabled, connected account in config order that
  can serve the request), or several accounts when pooling is on for them (see below).
- A key limited to some accounts (`--accounts`) is served only by those accounts. If none of them can answer, it gets an
  error, or, when the read allows backup sources, a labelled delayed answer from a data source; it never borrows another
  account's data or request budget.
- Orders always name their account. Portfolio reads (positions, holdings, funds, orders) are per account.

## 6. Pooling needs your consent

Pooling spreads read-only market-data calls (quotes, option chains, history) over several of **your own** accounts, so
each account's request limit is used. It is off by default. An account takes part only when it opts in
(`marketData.pooling`), names its `holder`, its broker's policy does not say `not-allowed`, **and you have accepted the
pooling notice for it**. The notice says in plain words that no broker's published terms clearly allow pooling and none
clearly forbids it, and that you are responsible for your brokers' terms. Accepting is a deliberate step:

- the dashboard shows the notice on the Sources page, with the accounts that could pool, and asks you to accept it;
- or from this computer with an admin key: `GET /v1/pooling` shows the notice and the accounts, `PUT /v1/pooling/consent`
  accepts it for the accounts you name, `DELETE /v1/pooling/consent` turns pooling off on the next read.

Only accounts of one holder are ever pooled together. Orders, positions, funds and other account data are never pooled:
they always use the account they belong to, from its own registered IP. Full details, the paid data plans some brokers
need, and what `mc-bridge doctor` checks are in [rate-limits.md](rate-limits.md).

## 7. Data beyond your accounts

Your broker accounts are the only real-time source. The Bridge can also read from free data sources and plugins you
switch on, and labels every answer from them as delayed or end of day. They never answer orders, risk checks, paper
fills or alerts. See [sources.md](sources.md).

---

<!-- docs/guides/rate-limits.md -->

# How the Bridge handles broker rate limits

Every broker API has request limits, and most are tight: often one quote request a second, sometimes one instrument
per call. Ten tools each polling on their own break those limits within seconds. The Bridge sits between your tools
and your brokers and makes the broker see one careful client. It also shares what it has fairly between your tools, and
says plainly why a request was held back. Reads can come from other sources than your brokers too; see
[sources.md](sources.md).

## The read path

For every market-data request, in order:

1. **Live stream.** If any client is streaming the symbol, the latest tick answers the request with
   `freshness.source = "stream"` and no broker call. One broker subscription is shared by every client (ten tools on
   one symbol cost one subscription). Feeds are opened per account, with each broker's subscription caps enforced
   (`SUBSCRIPTION_LIMIT` goes only to the client that crossed the cap).
   An **option chain** whose whole strike window (`strikes=N` around ATM) is live on the stream is built from those
   ticks over the day's broker chain, which supplies the previous-day OI behind OI change (`source = "stream"`, no
   broker call). Every reader of the same window (a dashboard page, your scripts) costs the broker nothing while the stream is up.
   A **quiet strike** (an illiquid far leg that has not traded) does not force a broker read: on a live subscription
   no tick means no trade, so its last tick is used while the feed is ticking now, the tick came on the current
   connection and it is at most `market.quietLegMaxAgeMs` old (60 s by default, 0 turns it off). Such legs carry
   `tickAgeMs`, and `freshness.quiet` counts them (`asOf` stays that of the live legs and the spot).
2. **Freshness cache.** A value younger than its freshness target is reused (`source = "cache"`). Defaults: LTP 1 s,
   quote 2 s, depth 1 s, option chain 3 s, expiries 5 min, history 1 min. Tighten them freely in `market.freshness`;
   they can be loosened only up to documented maximums. A caller may ask for fresher data with `maxAgeMs`.
3. **Coalescing.** Requests for the same thing that arrive while a broker call is in flight join that call instead
   of making their own. Twenty clients asking for the same price at the same moment make **one** broker call.
4. **Batching.** Symbols requested within a short window (25 ms by default) are combined into one call, up to the
   broker's documented batch size (for example 500 instruments per Kite quote call). A batch belongs to one API key (or
   tool): two keys asking for different symbols in the same moment make two calls, not one. That costs a few calls
   and keeps a light reader from waiting in a heavy reader's place in the queue. The same symbol asked by both
   still shares one call (step 3).
5. **Scheduling.** The call waits for budget in the account's token bucket for that endpoint class, in a fair queue
   (below).

When a read can also be answered by a source other than your own broker accounts (a free data source you switched on),
the Bridge's router decides which one, and a trace can show why. Streams and the cache always come first, and a
source never answers an order, risk check, paper fill or alert. See [sources.md](sources.md).

## Token buckets and priorities

- One bucket per **(account, endpoint class)**: `order`, `quote`, `depth`, `history`, `chain`, `portfolio`, `master`,
  `other`, with per-second, per-minute and per-IST-day windows as the broker documents them. Some brokers share one
  budget across several classes; that is modelled as a group bucket.
- Numbers come from the policy table, [server/bridge/ratelimit/brokerPolicies.mjs](../../server/bridge/ratelimit/brokerPolicies.mjs):
  one entry per broker, each figure with the URL of the broker's documentation and a `verified` flag. Anything not
  documented gets conservative defaults.
- Config (`ratelimit.brokers`, `ratelimit.accounts`) may only **lower** limits. A broker override above the table
  is a config error, so a typo cannot quietly raise a limit.
- Priority: `order` > `live` > `interactive` > `background`, with ageing so background work (instrument masters)
  still finishes under load. An order is never stuck behind reads.
- When a broker answers "too many requests", that account's budget pool backs off (below); other accounts carry on.

## Sharing fairly between your tools

Inside each priority, the queue shares the budget between **consumers**, one per API key (background jobs count as one
consumer each), instead of serving requests in arrival order. Each consumer has a **weight**, taken from the kind of
key (`ui` 4, `mcp` 2, `excel` 1, `script` 1, `other` 1, changeable under `ratelimit.client.kindWeights` or per key).
When two consumers compete, they get shares in proportion to their weights; when only one is asking, it gets everything.
So a spreadsheet that fires 500 requests waits behind an AI assistant's single question rather than in front of it.
Orders still go first: they are in a lane of their own.

Limits on one consumer: at most `queue.maxQueuedPerConsumer` (200) requests waiting, and while others also wait, half
the account's in-flight calls. When the queue is full the newest request of the biggest consumer is dropped, not
everyone's.

## When a broker says "too many requests"

A 429 from a broker pauses the whole **pool** that shares that budget (the classes of one account that share one
bucket), for the time the broker asks (`Retry-After`), else 1 s, 2 s, 4 s and so on up to `backoff.maxMs`, plus up to
250 ms of random jitter so tools do not return together. The Bridge never retries a throttled call itself.

After a throttle the Bridge also trusts its own table less. Each pool has a **scale** below the documented ceiling. A
throttle halves it (never below a quarter), and every clean minute with traffic gives back 5 percent. If the same pool
is throttled three times in an hour, it stays 20 percent below where it was for a day, and a warning says the table
figure is probably too high. The scale only lowers limits, never raises them above the policy, and lives in memory only.

## When the budget runs out

The Bridge never bursts past a limit. Instead:

- a cached value older than its target may be served, **labelled** `"stale": true` (up to `market.stale.maxStaleMs`,
  60 s by default; depth never older than 5 s);
- a symbol that could not be fetched in time is reported in `errors[]` with `UPSTREAM_RATE_LIMITED` and
  `retryAfterMs`, while the other symbols in the request are still answered;
- a request that cannot start before its deadline gets `429` with `Retry-After`.

**A refusal says whose limit it was.** Every 429 carries `scope`, `retryAfterMs` (the real wait) and `limit`
(`{ name, remaining, resetMs }`, the budget that said no):

| `scope` | Code | Meaning | What to do |
|---|---|---|---|
| `client` | `RATE_LIMITED` | This API key used up its own rate, its daily cap or its requests in flight | Slow this tool down, or raise its quota |
| `consumer-cap` | `RATE_LIMITED` | This key already has too many requests waiting for the broker | Send fewer at once |
| `queue` | `UPSTREAM_RATE_LIMITED` | The shared queue for that account is full | Try again shortly |
| `upstream` | `UPSTREAM_RATE_LIMITED` | The broker's budget cannot serve the request in time | Wait `retryAfterMs`, or use a cache or stream |

`Retry-After` is the same wait in whole seconds, rounded up with 0 to 25 percent added so waiting clients do not all
return in the same second. Clients should read the fields, not the text.

## Spreading reads across your own accounts (pooling)

If you have several accounts (at one broker or several), unpinned read-only market data can use the budgets of all of
them. This is called pooling. It is **off by default**, and turning it on is a decision you make, with your eyes open.

**What pooling is and is not.** It spreads quotes, option chains and history calls over your own accounts, so each
account's rate limit is used. It never moves an order: orders always go through the account they belong to, from that
account's own registered static IP. It never shares credentials, and it never mixes accounts of different people.

**Where the brokers stand.** No broker's published terms clearly allow pooling, and none clearly forbids it. Some say
things that could matter: Kotak and Shoonya say credentials are for the client's own use, Fyers bars use of its APIs
"by any third party", Motilal forbids using several keys to get around its order limit (a rule about orders, not
reads). The per-broker findings are in [BROKERS.md](../BROKERS.md#what-the-brokers-terms-say-about-pooling) and in
`poolingNote` on each entry of the policy table. You are responsible for following your brokers' terms. **A legal read
is recommended before you turn pooling on.**

An account takes part only when **all** of these hold:

1. it opts in: `"marketData": { "pooling": true }`;
2. it names its `holder` (`"self"`, `"spouse"` ...). Only accounts of **one** holder are ever pooled together;
3. the broker's policy entry says `pooling: "allowed"`, **or** the entry is `"unknown"` and the account also sets
   `"poolingWhenTermsUnknown": true`. A broker whose entry says `"not-allowed"` is never pooled;
4. **you have accepted the pooling notice for that account.** The notice is returned by
   `GET /v1/pooling` (the dashboard shows the same text). Accepting records `{ acceptedAt, version, accounts }` in `pooling/consent.json` in your data
   folder. A consent covers only the accounts you named, and it stops counting if the notice text changes (its version
   changes) until you accept the new text.

Today every broker's entry is `"unknown"`, so pooling needs both flags in the config file **and** your consent:

```json
{ "id": "upstox-main", "broker": "upstox",  "holder": "self", "marketData": { "pooling": true, "poolingWhenTermsUnknown": true } },
{ "id": "angel-main",  "broker": "angelone", "holder": "self", "marketData": { "pooling": true, "poolingWhenTermsUnknown": true } }
```

```bash
# read the notice and see which accounts could pool
curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $KEY" http://127.0.0.1:4300/v1/pooling
# accept it for two accounts of one holder (admin key, from this computer)
curl -X PUT -H "Authorization: Bearer $ADMIN_KEY" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{ "acknowledge": "pooling-1", "accounts": ["upstox-main", "angel-main"] }' \
  http://127.0.0.1:4300/v1/pooling/consent
# turn it off again; pooling ends on the next read
curl -X DELETE -H "Authorization: Bearer $ADMIN_KEY" http://127.0.0.1:4300/v1/pooling/consent
```

The notice you accept says, in plain words: pooling spreads read-only market-data calls across your own accounts; no
broker's published terms clearly allow or forbid it; you are responsible for your brokers' terms; orders always go
through the account they belong to from its own registered IP; where a broker needs a paid data plan every pooled
account needs one; and you can turn it off at any time. Consent is refused for accounts of different holders, unknown
accounts, paper accounts and brokers marked `not-allowed`. Accepting and revoking are written to the audit log.

The consent is one record for the whole Bridge. An admin key **limited to some accounts** can only change its own part of it:
accepting adds the accounts it names to the record (the others stay), and revoking removes only the accounts it may use and
deletes the record only when none are left. An unrestricted admin key (or this computer's control token) replaces or removes
the whole record. A limited key is never shown the other accounts.

**Paid data plans.** Some brokers charge for live data: Zerodha (Connect, Rs 500 a month per app), Dhan (Data API,
Rs 499 plus tax a month) and Groww (paid plan, Rs 499 plus tax a month). A pooled account without the plan cannot
serve live reads, and every pooled account needs its own plan. The policy table records this as `dataEntitlement`
(`free`, `paid`, `paid-for-live` or `unknown`, with a note and a source), and `mc-bridge doctor` warns about it.

What pooling does once it is on:

- **Many-symbol quote reads are split.** A request for 200 symbols is cut into each broker's batch size and every
  chunk goes to the pooled account with the most spare quote budget, so two accounts answer roughly twice as fast.
  An account in broker back-off gets no share.
- **Single reads** go to the pooled account with the most headroom.

`GET /v1/accounts` shows the effective `pooling` value per account (false until the consent covers it). `GET
/v1/pooling` shows, per holder, each account's broker policy, whether it opted in, whether the consent lists it and
whether it is pooled right now. Revoking the consent ends pooling on the very next read. Orders and portfolio reads are
never pooled, credentials are never shared, and accounts of different people are never pooled.

`mc-bridge doctor` checks the setup: it warns when an account is set to pool but has no consent (or only a consent for
an older notice), when a pooled account needs a paid data plan, when pooled accounts have different holders or none,
and when a broker's terms are unknown and `poolingWhenTermsUnknown` is not set.

## Broker plans (Fyers)

Some brokers have plans with different limits. Fyers has Standard (free: data calls 5 a second, 50 a minute and 5,000
a day, a live feed of 100 symbols) and Prime (paid: 10 a second, 500 a minute, 5,00,000 a day, 5,000 symbols), in
force since 16 October 2026. The Bridge assumes the lower plan. If you have Prime, say so per account:

```json
"ratelimit": { "accounts": { "fyers-main": { "tier": "prime" } } }
```

or for every account of the broker with `"brokers": { "fyers": { "tier": "prime" } }`. This is a choice among the
broker's documented plans, not an override that may only lower limits: pick Prime only if you have it, because the
Bridge cannot check your plan. An unknown plan name is refused for a broker entry, and for an account it falls back to
the lower plan. Limits you set under `brokers` or `accounts` still can only lower the figures of the plan you chose.

## Your own budget: quotas per key

Every API key has its own quota, so one runaway script cannot starve the others:

- `perSecond` and `burst`: a token bucket (default 50 a second);
- `perDay`: an optional cap on requests per IST day (no cap by default);
- `weight`: its share of a busy broker queue (see above);
- a cap on requests in flight at once (`ratelimit.client.maxConcurrent`, 64).

Set defaults for all keys under `ratelimit.client`, and per key under `ratelimit.client.keys.<keyId>`. You can also
change one key while the Bridge runs, from the dashboard (Sources, Quotas) or with an admin key from this computer:

```bash
curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $KEY" http://127.0.0.1:4300/v1/quotas            # every key: its numbers, usage and where they come from
curl -X PUT -H "Authorization: Bearer $ADMIN_KEY" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{ "perSecond": 5, "burst": 10, "perDay": 20000, "weight": 2 }' http://127.0.0.1:4300/v1/quotas/<keyId>
curl -X DELETE -H "Authorization: Bearer $ADMIN_KEY" http://127.0.0.1:4300/v1/quotas/<keyId>   # back to config or default
```

An override is kept in `quotas.json` in the data folder and sits above the config. Unlike broker limits, which a config
may only lower, a key's quota may be raised or lowered by you: it protects the Bridge from its own callers, not a
broker from the Bridge. Every response carries `RateLimit` and `RateLimit-Policy` headers (IETF draft format).

**Bounds.** A quota (in the config, or set through the API) takes finite numbers from 0.01 to 10,000 requests a second (one
request every 100 seconds at the least), a burst of 1 to 100,000 (a whole number), 1 to 100,000,000 requests a day (or `null`
for no daily cap) and a weight of 1 to 16. Anything else, including `NaN`, a negative number, a string or a rate like `1e-7`
that would lock a key out for months, is refused. The **only active admin key** may not be given less than 1 request a second
and 1,000 a day: a quota applies to the key, so one that is too small could lock you out of the API. **If a key is ever locked
out**, this computer's control token is not subject to any quota: run `mc-bridge` on this computer (the dashboard opened with
`mc-bridge open` works too) and delete the override (`DELETE /v1/quotas/<keyId>` as a local caller), or edit or remove
`quotas.json` in the data folder while the Bridge is stopped.

## Asking for less: stale-while-revalidate and prefetch priority

- `?swr=true` on `/v1/ltp`, `/v1/quotes` and `/v1/optionchain`: when only an older cached value exists (inside
  `market.stale.maxStaleMs`), it answers at once with `freshness.stale: true` and `freshness.revalidating: true`, and one
  refresh runs behind it (however many readers ask). The next read gets the fresh value from the cache.
- `?priority=background`: a prefetch. It waits behind every interactive read; a person's click on the same thing joins
  it and raises its priority. The dashboard prefetches this way when you hover a menu item or an expiry chip.

## Seeing it work

```bash
curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $KEY" http://127.0.0.1:4300/v1/limits                 # effective policy per broker, your key's budget
curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $KEY" "http://127.0.0.1:4300/v1/limits?explain=1"     # + the shared pools and who is waiting
curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $KEY" http://127.0.0.1:4300/v1/usage                  # per account and class: used, queued, back-off; savings
curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $KEY" "http://127.0.0.1:4300/v1/usage?series=1"       # + calls per second over the last two minutes
curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $KEY" "http://127.0.0.1:4300/v1/usage?view=budget"    # the dashboard's budget summary
```

`savings` counts the broker calls avoided today: served from stream, served from cache, coalesced and batched. Each
class lists every window (`windows`: this second, this minute, today) with what it holds now. Admin keys also get
`consumers`: today's broker calls and saved calls per dashboard page, API key (by label), MCP, Excel / compat and
background jobs.

`explain=1` adds, in numbers instead of log lines, why a request may have been slow or refused: `pools` (each budget
pool's accounts, spare room, ceiling, current scale and back-off, throttles in the last hour) and `consumers` (who is
queued or in flight and each one's share), plus `you`, your own key's quota and use. Other keys appear only to admin keys.

The dashboard shows the same figures. The **API** capsule in the top bar shows this second and this minute against the
limit, the stream and the calls saved today (fed by `budget` messages on the stream, op `subscribe_budget`). The
**Sources** page has the rest: **Overview** (how each source and account is doing, recent requests with what answered
each one, and a "Why this source?" check), **Providers** (switch sources on and off, keys, notices) and **Quotas** (each
key's share, with presets and usage). Recent requests are also `GET /v1/requests` on this computer; a market read there
carries `route`, a short record of what answered it (stream, cache, a shared call, a live call, or a stale value, with the
source, its data class and delay).

---

<!-- docs/guides/sources.md -->

# Data sources: where prices come from, and how the Bridge labels them

Your broker accounts are the Bridge's main source of market data. They give real-time prices and option chains, and they
are the only sources that orders, risk checks, paper fills and alerts use. The Bridge can also read from optional free
sources and from plugins you add. Those are slower or less certain, so every answer from them says so.

This guide is for people who use the Bridge. If you are writing a source, read [source-contract.md](../source-contract.md).

## What you get from each kind of source

| Kind | What it is | Is it on? |
|---|---|---|
| **Your broker accounts** (`builtin`) | Real-time prices, option chains, history, from your own login | Always on |
| **Bring your own key** (`byok`) | A data vendor where you hold the account and paste its API key | Off until you save a key and turn it on |
| **Opt-in** (`opt-in`) | Works without a key, but is unofficial or has strict terms | Off until you read a notice and say yes |
| **Plugin** (`plugin`) | Code someone else wrote, that you reviewed and approved | Off until you approve it |

There is no free, official source of real-time Indian market data that you may redistribute. Real-time prices and option
chains come from your broker. The other sources are for history, for a second opinion on a price, and for filling in
when no broker account can answer. They are labelled `delayed` or `eod` and are never mixed into a real-time answer.

## What the labels mean

Every price, candle and option chain the Bridge returns says where it came from. In the API this is the `freshness`
object; the dashboard shows the same words on a badge.

```json
"freshness": {
  "source": "backup",
  "provider": "yahoo",
  "asOf": "2026-10-19T09:45:00+05:30",
  "ageMs": 61000,
  "stale": false,
  "class": "delayed",
  "delaySec": 900,
  "official": false,
  "confidence": "low",
  "flags": ["unofficial", "delayed"]
}
```

| Label | What it means for you |
|---|---|
| `class: "realtime"` | From your own broker, or its live feed. Safe to act on. |
| `class: "delayed"` | The source is slow by nature, usually about 15 minutes. `delaySec` says how many seconds. The price is a real price from the past. |
| `class: "eod"` | End of day. You get yesterday's close, not today's price. |
| `official: false` | Not a documented API from the data's owner. It may change or stop without notice, and its terms may not allow what you do with it. |
| `confidence` | `high` for broker data. Lower for delayed, end-of-day, unofficial or flagged data. |
| `flags` | Extra warnings, for example `unofficial`, `delayed`, `eod`, `plugin`, `last-bar-provisional` (the newest candle is still forming). |
| `stale: true` | The value is older than the freshness target for that read. This is separate from delayed. |

**Delayed is not the same as stale.** A quote from a 15-minute source is `delayed`. It is not `stale` if you asked for
data that old. A broker quote that is two minutes old when you wanted two seconds is `stale` but still `realtime`.

**One value comes from one source, with one timestamp.** The Bridge never fills a missing bid from another source or
averages two sources. An option chain or a many-symbol quote takes the least current class of its parts, so one delayed
leg makes the whole chain `delayed`.

Excel and Google Sheets formulas see only the body of the answer, not headers, so the label is always in the body.

## Turning a source on

You need an admin key, or the dashboard.

**On the dashboard:** open Sources, then Providers. Each source shows what it gives, its limits, its terms and its
health. Turn it on there. For a source that needs a key, paste the key first. For an opt-in source, read the notice; saying
yes records the notice version and the time.

**From the command line:**

```sh
mc-bridge sources list                       # what exists, what is on, how each is labelled
mc-bridge sources set-key twelvedata         # asks for the key with hidden input (or reads it from stdin)
mc-bridge sources test twelvedata            # one small call to check the key and the vendor
mc-bridge sources enable twelvedata          # byok: needs the key first
mc-bridge sources enable yahoo               # opt-in: prints the notice and does nothing yet
mc-bridge sources enable yahoo --acknowledge yahoo-1   # after you read it: the version printed above
mc-bridge sources disable yahoo
```

`set-key` takes only the source id. A key typed after it (`set-key twelvedata MYKEY`) is refused, because it would sit in your
shell history. Commands that need an admin key read `MCB_ADMIN_KEY` (or `MCB_API_KEY`) from the environment; `--key <key>` still
works but prints a warning for the same reason.

Keys are never taken from the command line, so they do not end up in your shell history. They are stored encrypted on this
computer, never written to `bridge.config.json`, and never shown again, not even by the API.

If the notice changes, its version changes and you are asked again.

## The built-in sources

| Source | Kind | Gives | Limits the Bridge keeps to | Read this first |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Yahoo Finance | opt-in | Delayed quotes and history | 1 a second, 60 a minute | Unofficial. Yahoo's terms restrict automated access, so use it only for your own cross-checks. |
| Alpha Vantage | byok | End-of-day history and quotes | 5 a minute, 25 a day on the free key | Daily data only; intraday needs a paid plan. |
| Twelve Data | byok | End-of-day history and quotes | 8 a minute, 800 a day | Indian exchange data needs a paid plan; a free key is refused for Indian symbols. |

The numbers are the vendors' documented limits (or conservative figures where a vendor publishes none). The Bridge never
asks for more. Each notice shows the vendor's terms link and what you accept; the dashboard shows it before you turn a
source on. You are responsible for having the right to use a vendor's data.

In demo mode the Bridge also offers `demo-delayed` and `demo-eod` with sample data, so you can see every label without
a real source.

## When the Bridge uses a source

For a read that is not pinned to one account, the Bridge looks at the candidates and picks one:

1. It drops sources that cannot do the job: wrong capability, data too old for what you asked (`maxAgeMs`), not allowed for
   the purpose, circuit breaker open.
2. It prefers the candidate with the most spare budget, the lowest error rate and the lowest latency. It tries at most two
   candidates per request, so a failover is the retry.
3. Your live stream and the freshness cache are always tried first. Sources only add candidates; they never skip the cache.

**Purposes.** A read may say what it is for with `purpose`: `display` (default), `analysis`, `alert`, `paper`, `risk` or
`order`. The last four accept only real-time data from your own broker. A delayed or end-of-day source is never used for
them, whatever you configured, and neither is a cached value that has gone stale. Orders go through the account they belong to;
no source ever influences that.

The default, `display`, is for the public market routes: a `display` read may be answered from a cached value that is older
than its freshness target (labelled `stale: true`) when your broker's budget is used up, and from a backup source if the read
allows one. So code inside the Bridge never relies on the default. The order service (price band, market protection, strike
choice) reads with `purpose: "order"`, the paper engine with `"paper"`, and both check the label on what comes back: a value
that is stale, delayed, end of day, unofficial, from a source or unlabelled is not used as a price. A test scans the order,
paper, safety and compat code and fails if a market-data call there does not state its purpose.

**`maxAgeMs`.** If you ask for data no older than 2 seconds, a 15-minute source cannot answer, and you get your broker's
answer or an error, not a delayed price pretending to be fresh.

**Fallback.** When no broker account can answer (all logged out, all at their limit), the Bridge can answer from an
enabled source instead, but only if you allow it: the switch "Use free sources automatically when my brokers cannot
answer" on Sources > Providers (saved by the Bridge; `PATCH /v1/sources/settings`), `"sources": { "autoFallback": true }`
in the config, or `backup=true` on one request. The switch, once used, wins over the config. It is off by default. The answer carries the labels above, so you can tell.

A source that keeps failing is paused for a while (the Sources page says "Paused" and when it will be tried again),
and tried again after a cooldown that grows up to five minutes. A rate-limit answer, a bad key or an unknown symbol does
not pause it. A plugin that crashes is shown with its own reason.

To see why a source was or was not used, ask for a trace. It is a dry run: nothing is fetched.

```sh
mc-bridge sources trace --capability quotes --symbols NSE:RELIANCE --purpose display
```

```
Request: quotes NSE:RELIANCE, purpose display

CHOSEN    dhan-main              best spare budget (score 0.91, spare 0.8)
SKIPPED   yahoo                  delayed data cannot meet maxAgeMs 2000

Class of the answer: realtime. Served by your broker.
This was a dry run: no source was called.
```

## Seeing what answered a request

On the Sources page, **Overview** lists recent requests with a line for each: "answered from Dhan", "served from cache",
"used Yahoo, delayed 15 min". The same record is on `GET /v1/requests` (this computer only) as `route`:
`from` (`stream`, `cache`, `shared`, `live` or `stale`), the source and its name, the data class and the delay. For a
read of many symbols it is a summary, the least current verdict, never a list per symbol. The answer to the request
itself carries the full `freshness` label.

## How pooling and quotas fit

- **Pooling** spreads read-only market-data calls over your own accounts of one holder. It is separate from sources, off by
  default, and needs your consent (`GET /v1/pooling`, or the Sources page) because no broker's published terms clearly
  allow it. It never touches orders. See [rate-limits.md](rate-limits.md).
- **Source budgets.** Each source has its own budget from its documented limits, kept apart from your broker budgets. A
  free source never uses up your broker's request allowance, and a broker 429 does not slow a source.
- **Quotas.** Each API key has its own request quota and a weight in the queue, so one runaway spreadsheet cannot starve an
  AI assistant. A refusal says which limit tripped (`scope`: `client`, `upstream`, `queue` or `consumer-cap`) and when to
  try again. The dashboard (Sources, Quotas) and `GET /v1/quotas` show every key's share. `GET /v1/limits?explain=1` shows
  the shared pools and who is waiting.

## Plugins

A plugin is a read-only data source written by someone else, for example a vendor the Bridge has no built-in support for.
A plugin can answer quote, history, expiry and option-chain questions. It cannot place orders, log in, or see your
accounts, balances, positions or keys. Its data is always labelled `delayed` or `eod`, `official: false`, with the flag
`plugin`.

Treat a plugin as code you run on your computer, because it is. The Bridge limits what it can do:

- it runs in its own process with an empty environment, so it sees none of the Bridge's settings or secrets;
- all of its network access goes through the Bridge, and only to the https hosts its manifest lists and you approved;
- its files are pinned by hash, and a changed file is refused until you approve the change;
- it has call timeouts and request limits, and is stopped if it misbehaves.

These limits are real but not a complete sandbox. Node.js cannot stop a determined plugin from opening its own network
connection, and **a plugin runs as your user, so it can also send signals to the Bridge, for example kill it** (no setting
inside the Bridge can block that). Only use plugins whose code you have read or whose author you trust. If you must run one you
trust less, run it as another user (see "Running plugins as another user" below) or inside a container. [source-contract.md](../source-contract.md)
explains exactly what is and is not enforced.

To add one, in this order:

1. **Read** `mc-source.json` and the entry file (`index.mjs`). The folder may not contain symbolic links; the Bridge refuses it if it does.
2. **Pin** it: `mc-bridge sources plugins pin ./my-plugin` prints what you would grant (the hosts it may reach, its limits, its
   terms, the two files to read) and the pin.
3. Optionally **check** it: `mc-bridge sources plugins check ./my-plugin` runs its conformance checks offline. **`check` runs the
   plugin's code** on your computer (in the same restricted process and with a scripted network, but it is still its code), which
   is why it comes after you have read the files and pinned them, not before.

Then add it to the config:

```json
"sources": {
  "plugins": [
    { "path": "./my-plugin", "sha256": "<the pin>", "granted": true }
  ]
}
```

**Running plugins as another user.** If the Bridge runs as root on Linux or macOS (for example in a container or a service), you
can start every plugin as an unprivileged user so it cannot signal or kill the Bridge:

```json
"sources": { "pluginUser": { "uid": 1500, "gid": 1500 } }
```

The user must be able to read the plugin's folder. It is optional and never required. If it is set and the Bridge may not switch
user (it does not run as root, or the system is Windows), the plugins are **not started** and the log says why; they are never
quietly started with the Bridge's own privileges. A plugin is also never run as root. A plain desktop install runs as your own
user and cannot do this.

**If the Bridge was killed.** When the Bridge stops normally, on Ctrl+C or on a termination signal, it stops its plugin processes.
A forced kill of the Bridge (`kill -9`, the task manager's "end task", the out-of-memory killer) cannot clean up, and a plugin
stuck in a busy loop does not notice its connection closing, so it can keep running and using CPU. Find and stop it:

```sh
pgrep -af "plugin/child.mjs"      # Linux and macOS: lists the plugin processes
kill <pid>                        # then kill -9 <pid> if it stays
```

On Windows, look in Task Manager for `node.exe` processes whose command line contains `plugin\child.mjs`.

A plugin may have settings of its own; put them in a `config` object on its entry (the plugin's manifest says which keys
it takes, and a bad value stops it from loading). Never put a key there: a plugin's API key is saved from the Providers
tab like any other.

Restart the Bridge, then turn the plugin on like any other source. A plugin you granted but did not switch on is listed
as off. If you or anyone edits the plugin later, the Bridge
refuses it until you run `pin` again and update the line. A plugin that crashes four times in ten minutes is switched off,
and the reason shows in its health on the Sources page.

**Acknowledgements for opt-in sources.** Switching an opt-in source on needs you to acknowledge its notice. If you switch it off and
on again within 24 hours, one click is enough. If it has been off for more than 24 hours, or its notice changed, the notice is
shown again and the new acknowledgement is recorded (`needsAcknowledgement` in `GET /v1/sources` says which). At start, the Bridge
checks every source its state file marks as on: an opt-in source with no acknowledgement for the current notice is treated as off,
and a warning in the log names it. Those files (`sources/state.json`, the secrets store, the config) are **trusted local state, not
tamper-proof**: anyone who can write to the Bridge's data folder can change them, and the checks catch an honest mistake or a
restored backup, not a determined person.

## Configuration

```json
"sources": {
  "autoFallback": false,
  "timeoutMs": 5000,
  "pluginUser": { "uid": 1500, "gid": 1500 },
  "providers": { "yahoo": { "enabled": false } },
  "plugins": [{ "path": "./my-plugin", "sha256": "<the pin>", "granted": true, "config": {} }]
}
```

`pluginUser` is optional (see above). `autoFallback` is off unless you set it. `timeoutMs` is how long one call to a source may take (100 to 15000, 5000 by
default). `"enabled": false` under `providers` keeps a source off whatever the dashboard says. Whether a source is on, and the notices you acknowledged, are kept by the Bridge in
its data folder; use the dashboard or `mc-bridge sources` to change them. Keys are not config.

## Questions

**Why is a price 15 minutes old?** It came from a delayed source and the label says so (`class: "delayed"`). Real-time
prices come only from your broker. Log in to your broker account on the Accounts page.

**Can I use a delayed or end-of-day price for an order or an alert?** No. Orders, risk checks, paper fills and alerts accept
only real-time data from your own broker. This is enforced where the Bridge picks a source, and again by plugins refusing
those reads.

**Can I average a broker price and a free source to be safe?** The Bridge does not, and you should not. They are prices
from different moments. The Bridge keeps one value, one source, one timestamp.

**Why is Yahoo off by default?** It is unofficial and its terms restrict automated use. The Bridge makes you read that
before it is turned on. Treat what it returns as a cross-check, not as a price to trade on.

**Does a source use my broker's request limit?** No. Each source has its own budget.

**Is there a free real-time source?** Not one the Bridge can offer. Official real-time Indian market data is licensed. Use
your broker's.

**Where is my API key stored?** In the Bridge's encrypted secrets store on this computer, under the source's name. It is
never in the config file, never in logs, and never returned by the API.

**Can a plugin see my broker password or place an order?** No. It runs without the Bridge's environment or files, and its
protocol has no way to ask for accounts or orders. Order code never imports plugin code, and a test checks that.

**Can I pass this data to other people?** The Bridge is for your own use. Broker and vendor terms generally forbid passing
market data on, and the Bridge does not redistribute it. If you plan to share anything built on this data, get advice on
exchange data rules first.

**How do I see what a source did?** `mc-bridge sources list` shows health and last error; `mc-bridge sources test <id>` makes
one call; `mc-bridge sources trace` explains a routing decision.

---

<!-- docs/guides/paper-margin.md -->

# Paper margin: how the Bridge estimates it

**Approximate, not the exchange's SPAN.** The paper engine, the order preview and the margin route all use one function,
`portfolioMargin()` in `server/bridge/calc/span-margin.js`, so they always agree. Your broker's figure is the one that counts for live orders.

## What it does

Legs are grouped by underlying (NIFTY, BANKNIFTY, RELIANCE …). Within a group, longs, shorts and futures offset each
other, which is where a hedge earns its benefit.
