<!-- docs/guides/python.md -->

# Python

The Python client uses the standard library only (Python 3.9+), including its own small WebSocket client. Full
method list: [sdk/python/README.md](../../sdk/python/README.md).

```bash
pip install ./sdk/python
export MCB_API_KEY=mcb_...                 # a paper key for paper orders, a read key for data only
export MCB_BRIDGE_URL=http://127.0.0.1:4300   # optional; this is the default
```

## Market data

```python
from mrchartist_bridge import BridgeClient, BridgeApiError

bridge = BridgeClient()

r = bridge.ltp(["NSE:NIFTY", "NSE:BANKNIFTY", "NFO:NIFTY-2026-10-27-25000-CE"])
for item in r["data"]:
    f = item["freshness"]
    print(f'{item["symbol"]:40} {item["ltp"]:>10}  {f["source"]:6} {f["ageMs"]} ms{" (stale)" if f["stale"] else ""}')
for e in r.get("errors", []):
    print("not available:", e["symbol"], e["code"])

chain = bridge.option_chain("NIFTY", "2026-10-27", strikes=10)["data"]
candles = bridge.history("NSE:NIFTY", "5m", countback=300)["data"]["candles"]
```

## Paper orders

```python
try:
    res = bridge.place_order({
        "account": "paper", "symbol": "NFO:NIFTY-2026-10-27-25000-CE", "side": "BUY",
        "lots": 1, "product": "MARGIN", "orderType": "LIMIT", "price": 180,
    })
    print(res["data"]["orderId"], res["data"]["status"], "replayed" if res["replayed"] else "new")
except BridgeApiError as e:
    print(e.status, e.code, e.detail)          # e.g. 423 KILL_SWITCH_ACTIVE, 422 INVALID_ORDER
```

Every order write sends an `Idempotency-Key` (a fresh UUID unless you pass `idempotency_key=`), so resending after a
network error never creates a second order. A write that got no reply raises `BridgeConnectionError` with
`outcome_unknown=True` and is never retried automatically: check `orders()` or resend with the same key.

## Live stream

```python
with bridge.stream(["NSE:NIFTY", "NSE:RELIANCE"], mode="ltp", orders=True) as s:
    for msg in s:
        if msg["type"] == "tick":
            print(msg["symbol"], msg["ltp"])
        elif msg["type"] == "order":
            print("order", msg["order"]["orderId"], msg["order"]["status"])
```

## pandas

```python
import pandas as pd
c = bridge.history("NSE:RELIANCE", "1d", countback=250)["data"]["candles"]
df = pd.DataFrame(c)
df["time"] = pd.to_datetime(df["time"], unit="s", utc=True).dt.tz_convert("Asia/Kolkata")
```

<!-- docs/guides/typescript.md -->

# TypeScript and Node

A small client with no runtime dependencies (Node 20+), with TypeScript types in `src/index.d.ts`. Streaming uses
Node 22's built-in `WebSocket` or the `ws` package. Full method list: [sdk/node/README.md](../../sdk/node/README.md).

```bash
npm install /path/to/api-bridge-v2/sdk/node      # or: npm install ws  (Node 20/21 streaming)
```

```ts
import { BridgeClient, BridgeApiError } from "@mrchartist/bridge-client";

const bridge = new BridgeClient({ apiKey: process.env.MCB_API_KEY! });   // baseUrl defaults to http://127.0.0.1:4300

const { data, errors } = await bridge.quotes(["NSE:NIFTY", "NSE:RELIANCE"]);
for (const q of data) console.log(q.symbol, q.ltp, q.freshness.source, q.freshness.ageMs);

try {
  const { data: order, replayed, idempotencyKey } = await bridge.placeOrder({
    account: "paper", symbol: "NSE:RELIANCE", side: "BUY", quantity: 1, product: "CNC", orderType: "MARKET",
  });
  console.log(order.orderId, order.status, replayed, idempotencyKey);
} catch (e) {
  if (e instanceof BridgeApiError) console.error(e.status, e.code, e.detail);
  else throw e;
}

const stream = bridge.stream({ symbols: ["NSE:NIFTY"], mode: "ltp", orders: true });
stream.on("tick", (t) => console.log(t.symbol, t.ltp));
stream.on("order", (m) => console.log(m.order.status));
```

Same guarantees as the Python client: an `Idempotency-Key` on every order write, retries only where the Bridge says
an error is retryable, never a blind retry of a write (`BridgeConnectionError` with `outcomeUnknown: true`), the key
sent only as a header, and single-use stream tokens.

## Browser apps

A page served from another origin (for example a Vite dev server on `http://localhost:5173`) must be listed in
`cors.allowedOrigins`. Never put an admin or live key in browser code.

---

<!-- docs/guides/excel-sheets.md -->

# Excel and Google Sheets

Nothing a spreadsheet can call is able to place an order: every `/xl` route is a read-only GET. Full instructions and
Power Query files: [integrations/excel](../../integrations/excel/README.md),
[integrations/google-sheets](../../integrations/google-sheets/README.md).

## Excel for Windows: one value per cell

```bash
npx mc-bridge keys create --label excel --scope read --allow-query --client excel --expires 90d
```

Put the key in a cell on a hidden sheet and name it `BridgeKey`. With a symbol in `A2`:

| What | Formula |
|---|---|
| LTP | `=VALUE(WEBSERVICE("http://127.0.0.1:4300/xl/ltp?symbol="&ENCODEURL(A2)&"&key="&BridgeKey))` |
| % change | `=VALUE(WEBSERVICE("http://127.0.0.1:4300/xl/quote?symbol="&ENCODEURL(A2)&"&field=changePct&key="&BridgeKey))` |
| Open interest | `=VALUE(WEBSERVICE("http://127.0.0.1:4300/xl/quote?symbol="&ENCODEURL(A2)&"&field=oi&key="&BridgeKey))` |
| Safe | `=IFERROR(VALUE(WEBSERVICE(...)),"")` |

- The answer is a bare number (`.` decimal point, no grouping). In decimal-comma locales use
  `NUMBERVALUE(WEBSERVICE(...), ".")`.
- Any problem (unknown symbol, bad key, rate limit, Bridge not running) returns `#N/A` with an error status, so
  `IFERROR` catches it; the reason is in the `X-Error-Code` header (`curl -i`).
- These routes never use a backup data source (Yahoo, a plugin, ...), whatever `sources.autoFallback` says. A bare number or a
  fixed table has no room to say "this is 15 minutes old", and `WEBSERVICE` cannot see headers, so a delayed value would pass
  for a live one. `?backup=true` is refused with a message; for a labelled backup answer use the `/v1` routes. The freshness
  headers (`X-Data-Source`, `X-Data-Age-Ms`, `X-Data-Stale`) say when a cached value that has aged was served.
- Press F9 to refresh. Hundreds of cells are fine: repeated reads are served from the Bridge's stream or cache, and the
  broker only sees what is really needed.

## Tables with Power Query (Windows and Mac)

Power Query sends the key in an `Authorization` header, so a plain read key is enough. Paste
[`history.pq`](../../integrations/excel/history.pq) (candles) or [`chain.pq`](../../integrations/excel/chain.pq) (option
chain) into *Data → Get Data → Blank Query → Advanced Editor*, and choose **Anonymous** when Excel asks how to
connect.

```
http://127.0.0.1:4300/xl/chain?underlying=NIFTY&expiry=2026-10-27&strikes=10&greeks=true
http://127.0.0.1:4300/xl/history?symbol=NSE:NIFTY&interval=5m&countback=500
```

## Google Sheets

> **Compliance warning.** A tunnel to the main API makes a **public endpoint**, and your broker's data then passes
> through Google's and the tunnel provider's servers. Your broker's data terms may not allow that (**needs
> verification per broker**); the risk is yours. Excel on this computer needs no tunnel. See
> [compliance.md](compliance.md#tunnels-and-public-endpoints).

Sheets formulas and Apps Script run on Google's servers and cannot reach `127.0.0.1`. Run `mc-bridge expose sheets`: it
turns on a separate **Sheets listener** (`server.sheetsIngress`, port 4302) that serves only `GET /xl/*`, only for
read-only keys, with its own host list and a request cap. Point your tunnel at that port and at nothing else (never at
4300); the dashboard, `/v1` and every admin route do not exist on it. Make a read-only key with an expiry, limited to the
accounts the sheet needs. Anyone with the address and the key can read your data, so do not share the sheet. The steps,
the safe layout and the check are in [expose-alerts.md](expose-alerts.md#6-google-sheets). If you tunnel to the main port
anyway, requests that arrive through a tunnel (a host from `server.allowedHosts`, or any `X-Forwarded-For` / `Forwarded` /
`CF-Connecting-IP` header) are never treated as coming from this computer, but a read key then reaches far more than a
sheet needs; `mc-bridge doctor` warns about it.

[`bridge.gs`](../../integrations/google-sheets/bridge.gs) adds `=BRIDGE_LTP("NSE:NIFTY")`,
`=BRIDGE_QUOTE("NSE:RELIANCE","changePct")`, `=BRIDGE_CHAIN("NIFTY","2026-10-27",10)` and
`=BRIDGE_HISTORY("NSE:NIFTY","5m",100)`, sending the key in a header. Google refreshes custom functions only
occasionally, so Sheets suits slow dashboards, not live trading screens.

---

<!-- docs/guides/mcp.md -->

# AI assistants over MCP (Claude Desktop, Claude Code, Cursor)

The Bridge is an MCP server. AI assistants use the same broker connections, rate limits, safety checks and audit log
as every other tool, and they are **read-only by default**.

Two transports:

- **Streamable HTTP** at `POST /mcp` on the Bridge (this computer only; Host and Origin checked; bearer key).
- **stdio** through `mc-bridge mcp`, a relay that forwards each message to the running Bridge's `/mcp`. Start the
  Bridge first (`npx mc-bridge start`).

Create a key for the assistant:

```bash
npx mc-bridge keys create --label claude --scope read --client mcp
```

## Claude Desktop

Edit `claude_desktop_config.json` (*Settings → Developer → Edit Config*):

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "mr-chartist-bridge": {
      "command": "node",
      "args": ["/path/to/api-bridge-v2/bin/mc-bridge.mjs", "mcp"],
      "env": { "MCB_API_KEY": "mcb_..." }
    }
  }
}
```

On Windows use a path such as `"C:\\Users\\you\\api-bridge-v2\\bin\\mc-bridge.mjs"`. Restart Claude Desktop.

## Claude Code

```bash
claude mcp add mr-chartist-bridge --env MCB_API_KEY=mcb_... -- node /path/to/api-bridge-v2/bin/mc-bridge.mjs mcp
# or the HTTP transport directly:
claude mcp add --transport http mr-chartist-bridge http://127.0.0.1:4300/mcp --header "Authorization: Bearer mcb_..."
```

Check with `claude mcp list`. (Flags as of Claude Code's current CLI; see `claude mcp add --help`.)

## Cursor and other clients

Any MCP client that can run a command uses the stdio form (`node .../bin/mc-bridge.mjs mcp` with `MCB_API_KEY` in its
environment); clients that speak Streamable HTTP use `http://127.0.0.1:4300/mcp` with an `Authorization` header.

## Tools

| Toolset | Tools |
|---|---|
| `market` | `get_ltp`, `get_quotes`, `get_depth`, `get_history`, `get_expiries`, `get_option_chain`, `search_instruments`, `convert_symbol` |
| `analytics` | `option_chain_summary`, `history_summary` |
| `account` | `list_accounts`, `get_positions`, `get_holdings`, `get_funds`, `list_orders`, `get_order`, `get_safety_status` |
| `orders` (off by default) | `prepare_order`, `check_order_ticket`, `submit_confirmed_order` |

Every result is wrapped as untrusted data (instrument names and broker messages are third-party text) and carries
freshness labels.

## Letting an assistant prepare orders

Order tools appear only when all of these hold:

```json
"mcp": { "toolsets": ["market", "analytics", "account", "orders"], "orderAccounts": ["paper"] }
```

and the assistant's key has the `paper` scope (or `live`) and may use that account. Even then:

1. `prepare_order` only opens a **ticket**; nothing is sent.
2. You confirm the ticket on the dashboard (Pending confirmations) on this computer, within about a minute, or you
   **decline** it there (with an optional reason).
3. The confirmation gives a one-time code; `submit_confirmed_order` sends exactly the prepared order, once.

If you decline, nothing is sent and nothing can be: the ticket can never be confirmed afterwards. An assistant that asks
`check_order_ticket` with the `ticketId` gets a plain, machine-readable answer instead of silence:

```json
{ "ticketId": "tkt_...", "status": "rejected", "reason": "Wrong quantity", "canRetry": false, "nextStep": "..." }
```

`status` is `open` (you have not decided), `confirmed` (it needs your code), `consumed` (its order was already sent),
`rejected` (you declined; `reason` holds your words, which the assistant can read), `expired`, or `unknown` (the Bridge
does not know this ticket for this assistant; other assistants' tickets are never shown). Retrying
`submit_confirmed_order` for a declined ticket is refused with `STATE_CONFLICT` and `status: rejected`. Over plain REST
the same ticket ends as `CONFIRMATION_REQUIRED` when its confirmation code or `ticketId` is used.

No tool can change paper/live mode, key scopes or account sessions, or release the kill switch. Client-side approval
prompts never count as confirmation. AI-placed orders are a regulatory gray area; see [compliance.md](compliance.md).

> **What the confirmation step does not cover.** It stops an assistant that can only reach the Bridge through its
> MCP tools or its API key. It cannot stop an assistant (or any program) that can also **run shell commands or
> control the browser on your computer**, such as a coding agent with terminal access or a computer-use tool: such
> a program can read the Bridge's data folder, use the local CLI, or click Confirm on the dashboard for you. Give
> those tools a `read` key only, keep the `orders` toolset off for them, or run them in a sandbox or on another
> machine that cannot reach your Bridge's files or dashboard.

---

<!-- docs/guides/chatgpt-openai.md -->

# ChatGPT and OpenAI

## ChatGPT connectors

ChatGPT's connectors (custom connectors and apps) call MCP servers over the public internet, over HTTPS and usually
with OAuth. The Bridge keeps `/mcp` on this computer on purpose and has no OAuth server, so **ChatGPT cannot connect
to it out of the box**. Whether ChatGPT can reach a local MCP server in your setup **needs verification** against
OpenAI's current documentation.

Do not expose `/mcp` through a public tunnel to make this work. The public-ingress listener refuses `/mcp` by design
(it serves webhooks only), and `server.allowedHosts` plus a tunnel would put your account data one leaked key away
from the internet. If you do it anyway, put the tunnel behind your own identity-aware access control and use a
read-only, expiring key limited to the accounts you need.

## OpenAI function calling from your own script

The same tool registry is available as strict OpenAI function schemas:

```bash
npx mc-bridge openai-tools > tools.json                  # Responses API format, read-only tools
npx mc-bridge openai-tools --format chat > tools.json    # Chat Completions format
npx mc-bridge openai-tools --scope paper                 # includes order tools if mcp.toolsets/orderAccounts allow
```

Your script sends `tools.json` to the model and runs each tool call it gets back against the local Bridge, for
example through MCP's `tools/call`:

```python
import json, os, urllib.request

def call_bridge_tool(name, arguments):
    body = json.dumps({"jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 1, "method": "tools/call", "params": {"name": name, "arguments": arguments}}).encode()
    req = urllib.request.Request("http://127.0.0.1:4300/mcp", data=body, method="POST", headers={
        "Authorization": f"Bearer {os.environ['MCB_API_KEY']}",
        "Content-Type": "application/json", "Accept": "application/json, text/event-stream",
    })
    return json.loads(urllib.request.urlopen(req).read())["result"]
```

Order tools keep the same rule as everywhere else: they only prepare a ticket, and a person confirms it on the
dashboard before anything is sent. The Bridge itself never calls OpenAI.

---

<!-- docs/guides/expose-alerts.md -->

# Letting TradingView (and a Google Sheet) reach the Bridge safely

TradingView sends an alert from its own servers, and Google Sheets fetches prices from Google's servers. Neither can
reach a Bridge that listens on `127.0.0.1`. This guide shows how to open **one narrow door** for them without opening
the dashboard, and without breaking the static-IP rule for live orders.

The short version, on the computer that runs the Bridge:

```bash
mc-bridge expose alerts          # asks a few questions, writes the settings, prints what to paste
# restart the Bridge, start the tunnel, then:
mc-bridge expose check --public-url https://hooks.example.com --allow-outbound
```

Related: [webhooks.md](webhooks.md) (hook types and alert messages), [deployment.md](deployment.md) (static IP),
[vps.md](vps.md) (a hardened server), [safety.md](safety.md), [compliance.md](compliance.md).

## 1. The safe layout

The Bridge has up to three listeners. Only the two narrow ones may ever be pointed at by a tunnel or proxy.

```
  TradingView ---HTTPS 443--> [tunnel or proxy] --> 127.0.0.1:4301  alerts listener   POST /hooks/* only
  Google Sheet ---HTTPS 443--> [tunnel or proxy] --> 127.0.0.1:4302  Sheets listener   GET /xl/* only, read-only keys
                                                     127.0.0.1:4300  main listener     dashboard, /v1 API, keys, confirm
                                                                     ^ never reachable from outside
```

| Listener | Setting | Serves | Everything else |
|---|---|---|---|
| Main, port 4300 | `server` | The dashboard, the whole `/v1` API, key and order-confirmation routes | This is yours. Keep it on `127.0.0.1`. |
| Alerts, port 4301 | `server.publicIngress` | `POST /hooks/{source}/{token}` | 404 |
| Sheets, port 4302 | `server.sheetsIngress` | `GET /xl/*` for keys that are read-only | 404 |

What the wizard sets up, and what the check proves:

- A listener answers only to the host names in **its own** `allowedHosts` (plus `127.0.0.1`). A made-up host gets 403.
  The main listener's `server.allowedHosts` is not touched.
- A web page from another site (a browser `Origin` that is not allowed) gets 403.
- The alerts listener refuses a message over 16 KB (413). The Sheets listener takes no body and refuses any method but
  GET.
- The Sheets listener refuses any key with a scope beyond `read` (401) and limits each caller address to 600 requests a
  minute (`server.sheetsIngress.requestsPerMinute`).
- No listener accepts a WebSocket upgrade except where a route is marked public (none are on these two).

### What not to do

- **Do not point a tunnel or proxy at port 4300.** That publishes the API login to the internet. Dashboard pages still
  refuse other computers, but every key you have made would work from anywhere.
- **Do not set `server.host` to `0.0.0.0`** or turn on `server.allowNonLoopback` to "make the tunnel work". A tunnel on
  the same computer reaches `127.0.0.1`.
- **Do not add the tunnel's host name to `server.allowedHosts`** (the main listener). Add it only to
  `server.publicIngress.allowedHosts` or `server.sheetsIngress.allowedHosts`; the wizard does that.
- **Do not use `server.remoteDashboard`** outside a public demo. The Bridge refuses it with real accounts.
- **Do not put the key in a TradingView message.** TradingView says not to put credentials in the message body. The
  secret is in the webhook address; keep that address private.
- **Do not share the Sheets address, the sheet or its key.** Serving your broker's data to other people is outside the
  personal-use terms most brokers have ([compliance.md](compliance.md#tunnels-and-public-endpoints)).
- **Do not leave a quick tunnel running** after a test.

## 2. Where orders come from (the static IP rule)

SEBI's retail algo framework needs live API orders to come from a static IP registered with your broker (**needs
verification** against the circular and your broker's rules; see [compliance.md](compliance.md) and
[deployment.md](deployment.md)). A tunnel is **inbound only**: it carries TradingView's alert to the Bridge. The order
then goes from the Bridge to your broker **from the computer the Bridge runs on**.

```
  Home PC runs the Bridge, tunnel in front        VPS runs the Bridge (+ Caddy or a tunnel)
  TradingView -> tunnel -> Bridge (home PC)       TradingView -> VPS -> Bridge (VPS)
                              |                                           |
                              v                                           v
               broker sees your HOME address              broker sees the VPS's static address
               (changes unless your ISP gave a            register THIS address with the broker
               static IP) = live orders refused           = live orders accepted
```

- **Bridge at home, ordinary home connection:** alerts arrive and paper orders work. Live orders from that connection
  are refused by the broker unless your internet provider gave you a static address and you registered it.
- **A tunnel or forwarder on a VPS pointing at a Bridge on your home PC does not help.** It moves where alerts *enter*,
  not where orders *leave*. The broker still sees your home address, because the Bridge's own calls to the broker go out
  through your home connection. Only a VPN or exit node that carries the Bridge's outbound traffic changes what the broker
  sees ([deployment.md](deployment.md), option c).
- **Bridge on the VPS:** run the Bridge itself on the host that holds the registered address ([vps.md](vps.md)).

Set `live.registeredIp` on each live account so the Bridge's readiness check can warn you before an order fails.
`mc-bridge doctor` warns when a public listener and live trading are both on and that field is empty.

## 3. The three settings that make a listener safe

1. **`allowedHosts`** (on the listener): the exact host names it answers to, for example `["hooks.example.com"]`. No
   wildcards, schemes, ports or paths; the Bridge compares names exactly. A quick tunnel gets a new name each run, so it
   needs a new entry (and a restart) each run.
2. **`hooks.clientIpHeader`** (alerts only): behind a tunnel or proxy on this computer every connection comes from
   `127.0.0.1`. Name the header your tunnel or proxy fills with the caller's address and the Bridge will use it, but
   only when the connection itself comes from this computer, and it reads the **last** entry of `x-forwarded-for`.
   Without it, address-based rules see only `127.0.0.1`.

   | Provider | Header | Source |
   |---|---|---|
   | Caddy | `x-forwarded-for` | Caddy's `reverse_proxy` page: sets or augments it and ignores incoming values (read 2026-11-09) |
   | ngrok | `x-forwarded-for` | ngrok's HTTP docs: adds the client address, appending to an existing value (read 2026-11-09) |
   | Cloudflare Tunnel | `cf-connecting-ip` | **Unverified for Tunnel:** Cloudflare's header page says the edge sends it to the origin and does not mention Tunnel. Test it (section 7) |
   | Plain port forward | none | The Bridge sees the real caller as the connection address |

3. **`hooks.allowSourceIps`** (alerts only): a list of sender addresses; an alert from any other address is refused. It
   is the strongest protection for TradingView, which cannot sign its messages. The wizard offers TradingView's list:

   `52.89.214.238`, `34.212.75.30`, `54.218.53.128`, `52.32.178.7`

   These are the addresses TradingView's help page ([About webhooks](https://www.tradingview.com/support/solutions/43000529348-about-webhooks/),
   read 2026-11-09) lists. TradingView can change them: compare with that page now and then, and replace the list with
   `mc-bridge expose alerts --allow-ips a,b,c` (or edit `hooks.allowSourceIps`). **This list applies to every webhook
   of this Bridge**, including ChartInk and GoCharting hooks, whose senders have other addresses. If you use those too, leave
   the allowlist off here (`--allow-ips none`) and use per-hook `allowSourceIps`, or `requireConfirmation`.

TradingView's own limits, from the same page: it calls only **port 80 and 443**, cancels the call after **3 seconds**,
does not support **IPv6**, needs **2-factor authentication** on your TradingView account, and sends `application/json`
when the message is valid JSON and `text/plain` otherwise. Whether it can send custom headers is not stated there, so do
not depend on it. The Bridge answers an alert immediately (the order is processed after the answer), so the 3 seconds
is spent mostly on the tunnel.

## 4. The wizard: `mc-bridge expose`

```bash
mc-bridge expose                       # asks everything
mc-bridge expose alerts                # TradingView alerts
mc-bridge expose sheets                # Google Sheets
mc-bridge expose status                # what is on, in words
mc-bridge expose check                 # prove that only the intended routes answer (this computer only)
mc-bridge expose off [alerts|sheets]   # turn it off
```

Without questions (for a script or a server):

```bash
mc-bridge expose alerts --provider cloudflare --host hooks.example.com --yes
mc-bridge expose alerts --provider caddy --host hooks.example.com --allow-ips none --yes --check
mc-bridge expose sheets --provider cloudflare --host sheet.example.com --yes
```

| Option | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `--provider` | `cloudflare` (named tunnel), `cloudflare-quick` (testing only), `ngrok`, `caddy`, `port-forward` |
| `--host` | The public host name, for example `hooks.example.com` (a pasted `https://...` address is trimmed to the name) |
| `--port` | The listener's local port (default 4301 for alerts, 4302 for Sheets) |
| `--allow-ips` | `tradingview` (default for alerts), `none`, or a comma-separated list of addresses or IPv4 ranges |
| `--yes` | Ask nothing; fail with a clear message if something needed is missing |
| `--check` | Run the self-check right after writing (the Bridge must already run with the new settings) |
| `--public-url` and `--allow-outbound` | With `check`: also test the public address from this computer |
| `--json` | One JSON object instead of text |

What it writes: the listener (`enabled`, `host`, `port`, `allowedHosts`), `hooks.clientIpHeader` and
`hooks.allowSourceIps` for alerts, and `server.allowNonLoopback` only for a port forward. It keeps everything else in your
file, checks that the result loads before writing, saves the old file next to it as `bridge.config.json.bak-expose`, and
writes atomically. Running it twice changes nothing the second time.

**Restart.** The Bridge reads its settings once, when it starts, and does not reload them. After `mc-bridge expose`
(also after `off`), stop the Bridge (Ctrl+C in its window, or stop the service) and start it again. One restart covers
every change the wizard made. The wizard says so each time.

**Nothing is sent anywhere by the Bridge.** It never contacts TradingView, Google or a tunnel provider. The one outbound
request is the self-check's call to *your own* public address, and only when you pass `--allow-outbound` (the
dashboard never does it).

## 5. Provider recipes

Pick one. In each, run the wizard line first, restart the Bridge, then start the tunnel or proxy.

### A. Cloudflare Tunnel, named (recommended at home)

Needs a free Cloudflare account and a domain on it. The address never changes.

```bash
mc-bridge expose alerts --provider cloudflare --host hooks.example.com
cloudflared tunnel login
cloudflared tunnel create mc-bridge
cloudflared tunnel route dns mc-bridge hooks.example.com
```

Save `~/.cloudflared/config.yml` (use the id `tunnel create` printed; a sample with comments is in
[`deploy/expose/cloudflared-config.example.yml`](../../deploy/expose/cloudflared-config.example.yml)):

```yaml
tunnel: <Tunnel-UUID>
credentials-file: /home/<you>/.cloudflared/<Tunnel-UUID>.json
url: http://127.0.0.1:4301
```

```bash
cloudflared tunnel run mc-bridge
```

The commands are from Cloudflare's "create a locally-managed tunnel" page (read 2026-11-09). To keep it running after a
reboot, use Cloudflare's service install for cloudflared. The tunnel points at **4301**, not 4300.

### B. Cloudflare quick tunnel (first test only)

No account, but the name changes every run.

```bash
cloudflared tunnel --url http://127.0.0.1:4301     # prints https://<random>.trycloudflare.com
mc-bridge expose alerts --provider cloudflare-quick --host <random>.trycloudflare.com --yes
# restart the Bridge
```

Each new run needs the same two steps again. Do not use it for real alerts.

### C. ngrok (reserved domain)

Needs an ngrok account and a reserved domain.

```bash
mc-bridge expose alerts --provider ngrok --host your-name.ngrok.app
ngrok http 4301 --url https://your-name.ngrok.app
```

(`--url` is the current flag; ngrok's page marks `--domain` as deprecated, read 2026-11-09.)

### D. Caddy reverse proxy on a VPS

For the Bridge running on a VPS ([vps.md](vps.md)) with a domain pointing at it.

```bash
mc-bridge expose alerts --provider caddy --host hooks.example.com
sudo cp deploy/expose/Caddyfile.example /etc/caddy/Caddyfile
sudo systemctl edit caddy        # add:  [Service]  then  Environment=DOMAIN=hooks.example.com
export DOMAIN=hooks.example.com && caddy validate --config /etc/caddy/Caddyfile
sudo systemctl restart caddy
```

[`deploy/expose/Caddyfile.example`](../../deploy/expose/Caddyfile.example) answers only `POST /hooks/*` from the
TradingView addresses, 404 to everything else, caps the body at 16 KB and points at 4301. It is **untested** against a
real Caddy here: run `caddy validate` first. Open only ports 80 and 443 in the firewall.

### E. A plain port forward on your router (not recommended)

No HTTPS (the secret address travels unencrypted), your home address changes, and the Bridge has to listen on every
network interface. The wizard insists on the TradingView allowlist and refuses Sheets this way.

```bash
mc-bridge expose alerts --provider port-forward --host your-home-name.example.net
```

On the router forward external port 80 (TradingView calls only 80 and 443) to this computer, internal port 4301, TCP,
and nothing else. Never forward 4300. `mc-bridge doctor` will warn about the open listener. Prefer A or D.

## 6. Google Sheets

Sheets formulas and Apps Script run on Google's servers, so they need a public address. **The choice made here:** a
separate, optional, read-only listener (`server.sheetsIngress`, port 4302) that serves only `GET /xl/*`, for keys that are
read-only, with its own host list and request cap. A tunnel to it publishes nothing else. It reuses the same route rules
as the main port (the `/xl` routes and their key checks), refuses every other path and method with 404, and refuses a key
that has any scope beyond `read`. Pointing a tunnel at the main port, which the old Sheets instructions required, would
have exposed the whole API to anyone holding a read key; this does not.

```bash
mc-bridge expose sheets --provider cloudflare --host sheet.example.com
mc-bridge keys create --label sheet --scope read --expires 90d              # header key for Apps Script
# restart the Bridge, point the tunnel (hostname sheet.example.com) at http://127.0.0.1:4302
```

In Apps Script (*Project Settings, Script properties*, see [`integrations/google-sheets`](../../integrations/google-sheets/README.md)):
`BRIDGE_URL` = `https://sheet.example.com` (no slash at the end) and `BRIDGE_KEY` = the read-only key. The key is sent in a
header, not in the address. Use `--allow-query` only if you use `IMPORTDATA`, which puts the key in the address that
everyone who can open the sheet sees, and in Google's logs; `mc-bridge doctor` warns about URL keys with no expiry or one
longer than 90 days.

What is still true: the data passes through Google's and the tunnel provider's servers, and your broker's terms may not
allow that (**needs verification per broker**); the key is readable by anyone who can edit the script; there is no address
allowlist (Google's sending addresses are not something this guide can confirm). Excel on this computer needs none of this.

## 7. Test it

On the computer that runs the Bridge, after the restart and with the tunnel running:

```bash
mc-bridge expose check                                                    # this computer only, no outbound call
mc-bridge expose check --public-url https://hooks.example.com --allow-outbound
```

The first form probes `127.0.0.1` on each listener and confirms: the listener answers; the dashboard, `/v1` routes, keys,
orders, sign-in and spreadsheet routes (or, for Sheets, writes and webhooks) all answer 404; a foreign host name and a
foreign web-page origin get 403; an oversized alert gets 413. The second also looks up the host name and calls your public
address from this computer: it must reach the Bridge (not just the tunnel), the host must be on the list, the port must be
80 or 443, and the dashboard must not answer through it. Each failure comes with the fix. The verdict is **good**, **safe
with notes**, **not working yet** (the rules hold but the address does not reach the Bridge) or **unsafe** (turn the tunnel
off). The dashboard's Expose card (API, Integrations, Webhooks) runs the local part with one button.

Then send a real test: create a **paper** webhook (Dashboard, API, Integrations, Webhooks), paste its address into a
TradingView alert, and trigger it. In the Bridge's log, "hook refused: source address not allowed" means the sender list or
`hooks.clientIpHeader` is wrong for your provider (the quickest way to test the Cloudflare header); a 404 for the webhook
means the token in the address is wrong. Stay on paper until alerts arrive reliably.

## 8. Turn it off

```bash
mc-bridge expose off            # or: off alerts / off sheets
# restart the Bridge, then stop the tunnel or proxy
```

Also delete the webhooks you no longer use (dashboard) and the alerts in TradingView, and revoke the Sheets key
(`mc-bridge keys revoke <keyId>`). The settings stay in the file with `enabled: false`; `mc-bridge expose status` shows
the state.

## 9. What `mc-bridge doctor` checks

`mc-bridge doctor` prints each problem with a one-line **Fix**. `BLOCK` means it leaves the Bridge open to the internet or
makes a safety rule meaningless; `mc-bridge doctor --strict` then exits 1 (use it in a scheduler or monitor).

| Check | Raised when | Blocking |
|---|---|---|
| `expose-bind` | `server.host` is not loopback | with live trading or a public listener |
| `expose-dashboard` | `server.remoteDashboard` is on | outside demo |
| `expose-alerts-open`, `expose-sheets-open` | A public listener is bound to an open address | without a sender allowlist (and always for Sheets) |
| `expose-alerts-hosts`, `expose-sheets-hosts` | Listener on but no host name set | no |
| `expose-alerts-wildcard`, `expose-sheets-wildcard`, `expose-main-wildcard` | A host entry that can never match (`*`, scheme, path) | no |
| `expose-alerts-shared-host`, `expose-sheets-shared-host` | A tunnel host is also on the main listener | with live trading |
| `expose-client-ip` | A local tunnel with no `hooks.clientIpHeader` | no |
| `expose-allowlist` | Public alerts with no sender allowlist anywhere | no |
| `expose-live-alerts` | A live webhook with no `requireConfirmation` | also without any allowlist |
| `expose-static-ip` | A public listener, live trading and no `live.registeredIp` | no |
| `expose-url-keys` | A `--allow-query` key with no expiry or one over 90 days, with Sheets or a non-loopback bind | no |

## 10. When it does not work

| You see | Likely cause | Do |
|---|---|---|
| Check: "Nothing answered on 127.0.0.1:4301" | The Bridge is not running, or runs with the old settings | Start or restart it |
| Public check: the Bridge answered 403 | The host is not on the listener's `allowedHosts` | `mc-bridge expose alerts --host <name>`, restart |
| Public check: something answered, but not the Bridge | The tunnel is down or points at the wrong port | Check the tunnel and that it points at 4301 (or 4302) |
| Public check: name does not resolve | DNS record missing or still spreading | Wait a few minutes; check the record |
| TradingView shows a failed webhook, nothing in the log | Port other than 443/80, 3-second timeout, IPv6-only host, 2FA off | Fix per section 3 |
| Log: "source address not allowed" | The sender list or the client-address header is wrong | Check `hooks.clientIpHeader` for your provider, compare the list with TradingView's page |
| Every alert refused after you enabled the list behind a tunnel | No `hooks.clientIpHeader`, so every caller looks like `127.0.0.1` | Set it (the wizard does) |
| Live alert: `CANNOT_TRADE` | The broker session or the static address is not ready | The readiness badge says why ([deployment.md](deployment.md)) |

---

<!-- docs/guides/vps.md -->

# Running the Bridge on a VPS

For live trading, SEBI's retail algo framework needs orders to come from a **static IP registered with your broker**
(**needs verification** against the circular and your broker's rules; [compliance.md](compliance.md),
[deployment.md](deployment.md)). A small Linux server with a fixed IPv4 address is the most common answer. It also gives
TradingView somewhere to send alerts without a tunnel to your home. This guide is a hardened, ordinary setup: nothing in
it is specific to one hosting company, and every price, region and broker rule is yours to check.

**Status of the recipes.** The files in [`deploy/expose/`](../../deploy/expose/) were checked for syntax only: the systemd
unit with `systemd-analyze verify`, the compose file with `docker compose config`. The Caddyfile and the cloudflared
sample were not run against the real programs. Test each in your own setup, on paper, before real money.

```
   TradingView --HTTPS 443--> Caddy ----> 127.0.0.1:4301  Bridge alerts listener
   you (SSH, over WireGuard if you like) --> 127.0.0.1:4300  Bridge dashboard (never public)
   Bridge ----orders and data----> your broker      (the broker sees THIS server's address: register it)
```

## 1. Choose and prepare the server

- A VPS with a **static public IPv4 address** that stays yours (ask the host whether it can change, for example on a
  rebuild). Low latency to your broker helps; an Indian region is common (**needs verification**: location is a
  preference, not a rule here).
- Ubuntu or Debian LTS, 1 GB RAM is enough for one or two accounts. Node.js 22 or newer.
- Keep the clock right and set the zone: `sudo timedatectl set-ntp true && sudo timedatectl set-timezone Asia/Kolkata`.
  Order times, the 09:00 check and session expiries depend on it.

## 2. Harden it

```bash
# a normal user with sudo, and SSH keys only
adduser you && usermod -aG sudo you
# copy your public key to ~you/.ssh/authorized_keys, then in /etc/ssh/sshd_config:
#   PasswordAuthentication no
#   PermitRootLogin no
sudo systemctl reload ssh

# firewall: deny everything inbound except SSH and HTTPS
sudo ufw default deny incoming && sudo ufw default allow outgoing
sudo ufw allow 22/tcp          # or only from your own address: sudo ufw allow from <your-ip> to any port 22 proto tcp
sudo ufw allow 80/tcp && sudo ufw allow 443/tcp    # Caddy: certificates and alerts. Skip both with a tunnel.
sudo ufw enable

sudo apt install -y unattended-upgrades          # security updates
```

**Never open 4300, 4301 or 4302 in the firewall.** The Bridge listens on `127.0.0.1`; Caddy or a tunnel on the same
server is what the internet talks to. Docker can publish ports around `ufw`: the compose file below uses the host
network and publishes nothing.

Optional, a private way in: install WireGuard and give the SSH port only to the WireGuard address
(`ufw allow in on wg0 to any port 22`). The dashboard still goes through SSH (section 5), because its pages answer
only requests that arrive as this computer itself.

## 3. Install the Bridge

Either systemd (this section) or Docker (section 4).

```bash
sudo apt install -y git curl
# Node.js 22 or newer: install it the way your distribution or nodejs.org describes, then check `node --version`.
sudo useradd --system --home /var/lib/mc-bridge --shell /usr/sbin/nologin mcbridge
sudo git clone https://github.com/MrChartist/api-bridge-v2.git /opt/mc-bridge
cd /opt/mc-bridge && sudo npm ci --omit=dev

sudo install -d -o mcbridge -g mcbridge -m 700 /etc/mc-bridge /var/lib/mc-bridge /var/lib/mc-bridge-secrets
sudo -u mcbridge MCB_HOME=/var/lib/mc-bridge node /opt/mc-bridge/bin/mc-bridge.mjs init --config /etc/mc-bridge/bridge.config.json
```

`init` writes the settings file, a paper account and an admin key (shown once: save it). Then edit
`/etc/mc-bridge/bridge.config.json` so the data and the master key live in the folders the unit owns:

```json
{ "dataDir": "/var/lib/mc-bridge", "masterKeyFile": "/var/lib/mc-bridge-secrets/master.key" }
```

(`init` prints where it put the key: move that file to the path above, or set `masterKeyFile` to where it is.) Keep `server.host` at its default
`127.0.0.1`. Install and start the service:

```bash
sudo cp deploy/expose/mc-bridge.service /etc/systemd/system/    # check the node path on its ExecStart line (which node)
sudo systemctl daemon-reload && sudo systemctl enable --now mc-bridge
sudo systemctl status mc-bridge && journalctl -u mc-bridge -n 30
sudo -u mcbridge MCB_CONFIG=/etc/mc-bridge/bridge.config.json node /opt/mc-bridge/bin/mc-bridge.mjs doctor --strict
```

The unit runs as the `mcbridge` user, restarts on failure, has no extra privileges, a read-only file system except its
own two state folders and `/etc/mc-bridge`, and logs to the journal. Its header says what it expects.

## 4. Or with Docker

[`deploy/expose/docker-compose.yml`](../../deploy/expose/docker-compose.yml) runs the Bridge and Caddy in containers on the
**host network** (so the Bridge sees Caddy as a local proxy and trusts its `X-Forwarded-For`), read-only, without
extra capabilities, with the data and the master key in separate volumes. The Bridge listens on the server's loopback
only, so nothing but Caddy's 80 and 443 faces the internet.

```bash
export DOMAIN=hooks.example.com
docker compose -f deploy/expose/docker-compose.yml up -d --build
docker compose -f deploy/expose/docker-compose.yml logs bridge        # the first admin key, once
docker compose -f deploy/expose/docker-compose.yml exec bridge mc-bridge expose alerts --provider caddy --host "$DOMAIN" --yes
docker compose -f deploy/expose/docker-compose.yml restart bridge
```

The first start of the container makes a paper account and an admin key; add real broker accounts from the dashboard.

## 5. Reach the dashboard (never over the internet)

From your own computer, with an SSH tunnel:

```bash
ssh -L 4300:127.0.0.1:4300 you@your-vps
```

Leave it open and browse to `http://127.0.0.1:4300/dashboard` on your computer. To sign in without typing a key, run
`mc-bridge open` on the server (as the service user, with the same `MCB_CONFIG`): with no browser there it prints a one-time link starting `http://127.0.0.1:4300/dashboard#signin=`;
open that link in your own browser while the tunnel is up. Close the tunnel when you are done.

Why not WireGuard straight to the dashboard? Dashboard pages and every admin or order-confirmation route answer only a
request that reaches the Bridge as **this computer** (a loopback connection to a loopback name). A connection from a
WireGuard address is not that, so it is refused by design. SSH, even over WireGuard, ends on the server's own loopback.

## 6. Let TradingView in

Follow [expose-alerts.md](expose-alerts.md): run `mc-bridge expose alerts --provider caddy --host hooks.example.com`
(as the service user on a systemd install), copy [`Caddyfile.example`](../../deploy/expose/Caddyfile.example) to
`/etc/caddy/Caddyfile`, restart the Bridge, then `mc-bridge expose check --public-url https://hooks.example.com --allow-outbound`.

## 7. Register the static address, and plan changes

1. Find the server's public IPv4 address (your host's control panel shows it; or `curl -4 https://api.ipify.org` on the
   server, which asks that service).
2. Register it in your broker's API settings as the **primary** address (**needs verification**: where and how, per
   broker; most also accept one backup).
3. Put it in the account: `"live": { "enabled": true, "allowedSources": ["rest", "webhook"], "registeredIp": "<address>" }`.
4. Turn on the readiness lookup ([deployment.md](deployment.md), section 4) so the Bridge notices a different address
   within minutes.

**Brokers limit how often the registered address can change** (some allow one change a week; **needs verification** per
broker), and a change may take effect after a delay. So plan it:

| When | Steps |
|---|---|
| You are moving to a new server | Outside market hours. (1) Build and test the new server on **paper**. (2) Register its address as the **backup** with the broker, if the broker has one, and set `live.backupIp`. (3) Wait until the broker shows it as accepted. (4) Switch the DNS record or tunnel to the new server and run the check. (5) Make it the primary when the broker allows, update `live.registeredIp` and `backupIp`. (6) Run `mc-bridge doctor --strict` and look at the readiness badge. (7) Stop the old server. Keep the **kill switch** on while the two overlap so only one Bridge can send orders. |
| The server's address changed by itself | The readiness badge shows `IP_MISMATCH` within about 5 minutes and automated live orders are refused. Engage the kill switch (`mc-bridge kill`), ask the host for the old address back or register the new one (mind the broker's change limit), update `live.registeredIp`, release the kill switch. |
| You rebuild the server | Ask the host to keep the address; take a copy first (section 9). |

Never run two Bridges with live trading on at once: each has its own order counters and daily limits.

## 8. Updating

```bash
cd /opt/mc-bridge
sudo systemctl stop mc-bridge
# take a copy first (section 9), and read CHANGELOG.md for what changed
sudo git pull --ff-only && sudo npm ci --omit=dev
sudo systemctl start mc-bridge
sudo -u mcbridge MCB_CONFIG=/etc/mc-bridge/bridge.config.json node bin/mc-bridge.mjs doctor --strict
```

With Docker: `docker compose -f deploy/expose/docker-compose.yml build --pull && docker compose -f deploy/expose/docker-compose.yml up -d`.
Update outside market hours, then look at the readiness badge and send a paper order.

## 9. Backups

The Bridge has no backup command. Everything it keeps is in two places, and they should be backed up **separately**:

- the **data folder** (`/var/lib/mc-bridge`, or the `bridge-data` volume): keys (hashed), settings of hooks, the audit log
  and the encrypted broker secrets;
- the **master key** (`/var/lib/mc-bridge-secrets/master.key`, or the `bridge-secrets` volume) and `/etc/mc-bridge/bridge.config.json`.

A copy of the data without the key is useless to a thief, and a copy of the key without the data is too; keep them in
different places. For a copy that is consistent, stop the service, copy, start it. Practice a restore on a spare machine
before you need it. Broker sessions are not restored: you log in again.

## 10. Keep an eye on it

- `journalctl -u mc-bridge -f` (or `docker compose logs -f bridge`) for the log; keys never appear in it.
- A daily check from cron or a systemd timer: `mc-bridge doctor --strict` exits 1 when something blocks. Send its output
  by mail or to your own monitor.
- Log in to your broker every morning (the Bridge never automates it) and look at the readiness badge: a forgotten login is
  the most common reason an alert is refused ([deployment.md](deployment.md), section 5).

## Checklist

- [ ] SSH keys only, root login off, firewall allows only 22 (or WireGuard), 80 and 443.
- [ ] `server.host` is `127.0.0.1`; nothing listens publicly except Caddy (`ss -ltnp` shows 4300, 4301, 4302 on 127.0.0.1).
- [ ] `mc-bridge doctor --strict` exits 0; `mc-bridge expose check --public-url ... --allow-outbound` says good.
- [ ] The server's address is registered with the broker and set as `live.registeredIp`; the readiness lookup is on.
- [ ] Live hooks use `requireConfirmation` or a sender allowlist; you tested on paper first.
- [ ] Data and master key are backed up in different places, and a restore has been tried.

---

<!-- docs/guides/deployment.md -->

# Deployment: static IP, daily login and the readiness check

Paper trading works from any computer and any connection. **Live API orders do not.** This guide explains why, the
ways to give the Bridge a fixed internet address, and how the Bridge's trading-readiness check tells you, before an
order fails, that something is wrong.

Every rule below that comes from SEBI, an exchange or a broker is marked **needs verification**: check it against your
broker's current rules before you rely on it. See also [compliance.md](compliance.md) and [safety.md](safety.md).

## 1. Why it matters

- SEBI's retail algo framework (in force from 1 April 2026; **needs verification**) requires API **orders** to come
  from a **static IP address registered with your broker**: one primary address and, at most brokers, one backup.
  Brokers refuse an API order from any other address.
- Data calls (quotes, chains, positions) generally work from anywhere. Only orders are checked (**needs
  verification** per broker).
- A normal home connection or a mobile hotspot has a **dynamic** address that changes after a router restart, a
  power cut or at the provider's will. From such a connection, live orders will be refused, and you find out only
  when one is.
- Brokers also log API sessions out every day (the "daily logout"; **needs verification** per broker). You log in
  each morning; the Bridge never automates logins or two-factor codes.

## 2. Options for a fixed address

| Option | What you do | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| (a) Static IP from your internet provider | Ask your ISP for a static IPv4 address for your home connection and run the Bridge on your PC | Cost and availability vary by provider and city; ask the ISP |
| (b) A small Linux VPS in India | Rent a server with a static IPv4 address, install the Bridge there ([install.md](install.md)), keep it on `127.0.0.1` and reach the dashboard from your own computer with `ssh -L 4300:127.0.0.1:4300 you@your-vps` | Monthly cost is modest at most hosts (**needs verification**); pick an Indian region for low latency |
| (c) A VPN or exit node with a dedicated IP | Route the Bridge's traffic through a VPN that gives you your own fixed exit address | The broker sees the **exit** address, so register that one. Split tunnels can send broker traffic another way: check |

**Never put a public tunnel (ngrok, Cloudflare Tunnel and similar) in front of a Bridge that holds `live` keys.** A
tunnel does not give the broker a fixed address (it is inbound only: orders still leave from the computer the Bridge runs
on), and a tunnel to the main port exposes your API to the internet. TradingView alerts and Google Sheets have their own
narrow public listeners for that, with a wizard and a check: [expose-alerts.md](expose-alerts.md). A hardened server
recipe is in [vps.md](vps.md).

## 3. Register the address with your broker, then tell the Bridge

1. Find your public address on the machine that runs the Bridge (for example, open `https://api.ipify.org` in a
   browser on that machine).
2. Register it in your broker's API settings (the developer or API-key page at Dhan, Zerodha Kite Connect and Upstox;
   **needs verification**: menu names change).
3. Put the same address in `bridge.config.json` for that account:

```json
{
  "id": "dhan-main",
  "broker": "dhan",
  "live": { "enabled": true, "allowedSources": ["rest"], "registeredIp": "203.0.113.10", "backupIp": "203.0.113.11" }
}
```

`mc-bridge doctor` warns about any live-enabled account without `live.registeredIp`.

## 4. Turn on the readiness lookup

The Bridge cannot know its own public address; only an outside service can echo it back. So the check is **off by
default**. Turn it on in `bridge.config.json`:

```json
"readiness": { "egressIp": { "mode": "lookup", "lookupUrl": "https://api.ipify.org" } }
```

- Choose an **IPv4-only** service: brokers register IPv4 addresses, and an answer over IPv6 cannot be compared (the
  check then shows "IP family differs", a warning, not a failure).
- **The service you choose sees your IP address** every time the Bridge asks: once per check, every 4 minutes from
  08:45 to 15:45 IST on trading days. The Bridge keeps the answer in memory only, never writes it to disk, and never
  puts it in notifications, logs or MCP results.
- Its answer can differ from what your broker sees (dual WAN, a VPN split tunnel). The dashboard always says "as seen
  by <service>".
- `"mode": "manual"` with `"manualIp"` records the address you state. It can never notice a change.

## 5. The daily routine and what the badge means

Every page of the dashboard has a **trading-readiness badge** in the toolbar (on phones, a power icon with a dot).
Click it for the detail; the Safety page has the full card, the last changes and a **Check now** button.

| Badge | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Ready | Every live account passed: session, static IP, order headroom, daily limits, kill switch |
| Check: … | Something needs a look but orders can still go (a session that ends before the close, a daily loss limit that is nearly used, the lookup is off) |
| Cannot trade: … | At least one live account would have its orders refused. Automated live orders (webhooks) on that account are refused with `CANNOT_TRADE`; orders you send yourself carry a warning |
| Paper only | No account has live trading on |
| Not checked since … | Outside market hours the Bridge does not call the broker, so the reading gets old by design |

The routine:

1. Log in to each broker in the morning (Accounts page, or `mc-bridge accounts connect <id>`).
2. At **09:00 IST** on trading days the Bridge checks every live account and flags any that is not
   ready on the badge and in `GET /v1/readiness`.
3. During the day it checks every 4 minutes, and at once when a session changes, a broker refuses a session or the
   kill switch moves. A changed address is noticed within 5 minutes.

## 6. Clock

Keep automatic time (NTP) on. Order times, the 09:00 check and session expiries all depend on the clock. With the
lookup on, the readiness card warns when the clock is off by more than 5 seconds.

## 7. Phones

Reach the dashboard from your phone over your own VPN (WireGuard, Tailscale) or an SSH tunnel, never a public tunnel.
The badge works the same on a phone: a power icon with a dot, and a bottom sheet with the detail.

## 8. Troubleshooting

| Reason | What it means | What to do |
|---|---|---|
| `SESSION_EXPIRED`, `SESSION_MISSING`, `SESSION_REJECTED` | The broker session is gone or was refused | Log in again: `mc-bridge accounts connect <id>`, or the Accounts page |
| `SESSION_EXPIRES_SOON` | The broker's stated expiry is before the close | Log in again before it ends |
| `PROBE_FAILED` | A read call to the broker failed (timeout, broker error) | Usually passes by itself; check the broker's status page |
| `IP_MISMATCH` | The looked-up address is not the registered one | Check the connection or VPN; if your address changed for good, register the new one with the broker and in `live.registeredIp` |
| `IP_NOT_REGISTERED`, `IP_INVALID_CONFIG` | `live.registeredIp` is missing or not a valid address | Set it (section 3) |
| `IP_UNCHECKED` | The lookup is off | Turn it on (section 4), or accept that a change is found only when an order is refused |
| `IP_LOOKUP_FAILED` | The lookup service did not answer | Check the URL; choose another service |
| `IP_FAMILY_DIFFERS` | The service answered over IPv6 | Use an IPv4-only lookup URL |
| `CLOCK_SKEW` | This computer's clock is off | Turn on automatic time |
| `DAILY_ORDERS_LOW`, `DAILY_ORDERS_EXHAUSTED` | Few or no orders left today | The count resets at midnight IST |
| `DAILY_LOSS_NEAR`, `DAILY_LOSS_REACHED` | The daily loss limit is nearly or fully used | It resets at midnight IST |
| `KILL_SWITCH` | The kill switch is on | Release it on the Safety page if this was not intended |
| `RATE_CAP_REACHED`, `BROKER_ORDER_BACKOFF` | The order-rate cap is in use, or the broker asked to slow down | Passes within seconds |

Escape hatches, if the check itself gets in the way: `"readiness": { "gateAutomated": false }` turns the refusal of
automated orders into a warning, and `"readiness": { "enabled": false }` turns the checks off.

---

<!-- docs/guides/safety.md -->

# Safety model

The Bridge is built so that a mistake (a buggy script, a runaway alert, a confused AI assistant, a leaked key) costs
as little as possible. Everything below is on by default.

## Paper first

- Every order, webhook and AI tool is **paper** unless it explicitly asks for live. Each order result says
  `"mode": "paper"` or `"live"`.
- The `paper` account (and paper mode on any account) is a local simulator priced from real market data: ₹10,00,000
  starting capital, fills at the opposite best price or LTP ± slippage, intraday square-off at 15:20 IST, simple margin
  approximations (not a broker's SPAN). `POST /v1/paper/accounts/{id}/reset` starts over.

## Live orders need every one of these

1. `"safety": { "liveTrading": true }` in `bridge.config.json`;
2. the account's `"live": { "enabled": true }`;
3. the request source (`rest`, `webhook`, `mcp` or `cli`) listed in that account's `live.allowedSources`
   (`["rest"]` by default);
4. an API key with the `live` scope (created from this computer only);
5. `"mode": "live"` in the request;
6. human confirmation for AI assistants and for hooks with `requireConfirmation`. "AI assistant" means a key created
   with `--client mcp`, on **every** route (REST included), not only the MCP endpoint; such a key cannot have the
   admin scope, and the client that prepared a ticket can never confirm it. The person can also **decline** a ticket
   (see below);
7. an `Idempotency-Key` header or a `clientOrderId` (a live order without one is refused, so a retry cannot double it);
8. every safety check below.

A request that misses any of them is refused with a clear code, never quietly downgraded. Nothing in the API, the
environment (`MCB_PAPER_ONLY=1` can only tighten), an MCP tool or a webhook can switch live trading on.

### Trading readiness

The Bridge checks every live-enabled account at 09:00 IST on trading days and every 4 minutes from 08:45 to 15:45
IST: broker session (stated expiry plus a cheap read call), this computer's IP against `live.registeredIp` (only when
you turn the lookup on), order-rate and daily headroom, and the kill switch. Each account is `ready`, `warn`,
`cannot_trade`, `paper_only` or `unknown`. `GET /v1/readiness` returns it; the dashboard shows it as a badge on every
page and a card on the Safety page; `get_safety_status` (MCP) includes it.

| Order | While its account is `cannot_trade` |
|---|---|
| Automated live order (webhook) | **Refused** with `CANNOT_TRADE`; no broker call is made. A stale reading is refreshed first (up to 5 s) |
| Live order a person sends (REST, CLI, a confirmed MCP ticket) | Sent through the usual checks, with a `READINESS` warning |
| Paper order | No readiness line (paper never needs the broker session) |

Readiness only adds a refusal or a warning: it never engages the kill switch, cancels or sends anything. Turn the
refusal into a warning with `readiness.gateAutomated: false`. Static IP and the daily login are explained in
[deployment.md](deployment.md).

## Checks on every order (paper and live)

| Check | Default |
|---|---|
| Kill switch | Off. `POST /v1/safety/kill-switch` from any key, with an empty body or `{"reason": "..."}`, stops every new order at once, including orders already waiting in the queue and the remaining parts of a sliced order (checked again right before each is sent). `"cancelOpenOrders": true` needs a `live` key (or admin on this computer) and cancels only orders the Bridge placed, on the accounts that key may use; `"includeExternal": true` (admin on this computer) also cancels orders placed outside the Bridge, such as protective stop-losses. Release: admin key, this computer, `DELETE /v1/safety/kill-switch {"confirm": "RELEASE"}`. `mc-bridge kill` / `mc-bridge kill release` from the terminal, with no key needed on the computer running the Bridge (it reads the owner-only `control.token` the Bridge keeps in its data folder while it runs; the token works only for the kill switch, from this computer). `MCB_KILL_SWITCH=1` or `safety.killSwitchOnStart` engages it at start. |
| Order rate | 5 per second per account (place, modify and cancel all count), taken when the order actually leaves for the broker, so orders that queued behind a broker back-off cannot burst above it. Paper orders are paced at the same rate in their own window. Config cannot set more than 10 (see [compliance.md](compliance.md)). Kept per Bridge account: two entries for the same broker login each get their own cap (**needs verification**: per client, per PAN or per exchange). |
| Daily orders | 100 per account per IST day; an order that passes its checks reserves its place at once (so concurrent requests cannot overshoot), and each slice of a sliced order counts as one |
| Daily loss | ₹10,000 per account per IST day. Paper: realised P&L from the paper engine's fills. Live: the broker's day P&L (realised plus open positions) read before each live order; when it cannot be read the order carries a warning that the limit was not checked |
| Order value | ₹2,00,000. A modify is checked on the order after the change: the new quantity × the new limit (or trigger) price, or × LTP for a market order |
| Lots per order | 10, on every place and every modify (paper and live) |
| Price band | Limit and trigger prices within 3% of LTP, on every place and every modify, paper and live (a live modify without an LTP is refused) |
| Market orders | `protect`: sent as a limit order at LTP ± 2% (or the broker's native protection); `reject`: refused |
| Market hours | Live orders outside NSE/BSE hours are refused; MCX (09:00 to 23:55) and CDS (09:00 to 17:00) by weekday window (**needs verification**, holidays not known); paper orders only warn |
| Unverified live adapters | Live orders on brokers verified only against fixtures (today Zerodha and Upstox) carry a warning on every preview and place |
| Freeze quantity | Orders above the exchange freeze quantity are refused (or sliced, if `orders.sliceAboveFreeze` is on). A modify cannot be sliced, so a change above the freeze quantity is refused |

A modify, paper or live, passes every check in this table on the order as it would stand after the change, except
the daily order count and daily loss (it changes an order already counted). Cancels pass none of them except the order
rate, so risk can always be reduced.

Per-account `limits` may be stricter than the global `safety` values, never looser. `GET /v1/safety` shows today's
counters.

## Idempotency

Send an `Idempotency-Key` header on every write (the SDKs do it for you); live orders without it (or a
`clientOrderId`) are refused. The same key, from the same key holder,
never reaches a broker twice; a repeat returns the first result with `Idempotency-Replayed: true`. A live call that
times out becomes `outcome_unknown`; the Bridge then checks the broker's order book and updates the order. It never
retries an order write blindly.

## Keys

- Format `mcb_<keyId>_<secret>`; only `scrypt(secret)` is stored (`data/keys.json`). The key is shown once.
- Scopes: `read` (data, portfolio, orders list) < `paper` (+ paper orders) < `live` (+ live orders); `admin` (+ keys,
  audit, sessions, hooks, confirmations, kill-switch release), most admin actions from this computer only.
- Effective hierarchy: `admin` implies `read` only, **not** `paper` or `live`. A key can never grant more than it
  holds where it matters: creating a `live` key, or a webhook with `"mode": "live"`, needs a key that has `live`
  itself (an admin key pasted into the dashboard cannot open a live trading path on its own). The CLI, run on this
  computer, is not limited. `key.created` and `hook.created` audit records name the creating key.
- Malformed keys and unknown key ids are refused without any hashing; at most two scrypt checks run at a time, and an
  address that sends 30 bad keys in a minute is refused for the rest of that minute.
- Optional account list and expiry per key. `mc-bridge keys revoke <id>` takes effect on the next request and closes
  the key's open streams.
- `?key=` in a URL only for read-only keys created with `--allow-query` (Excel, AmiBroker).

## Network

- Binds `127.0.0.1`. Binding anything else needs `server.allowNonLoopback: true` in the file, and keys are still
  required everywhere.
- Host header allowlist (blocks DNS rebinding: a web page cannot point its own name at `127.0.0.1` and talk to the
  Bridge). Origin allowlist for browsers (`cors.allowedOrigins`, no wildcard). The dashboard calls its own origin.
- The optional public-ingress listener serves webhook routes only.

## Secrets

- Broker credentials: AES-256-GCM per entry (fresh 12-byte IV per write, entry name as associated data), an HMAC over
  the whole file to catch tampering or rollback, atomic writes. A tampered file is refused, never partly read.
- Master key: `MCB_MASTER_KEY` (base64 of 32 bytes), or `MCB_MASTER_KEY_FILE` / `data/master.key`, created with mode
  `600` on first start; a key file readable by other users is refused. Back it up: without it the saved broker logins
  cannot be read (you can always log in again).
- Keep the master key **out of the data folder**. The default `data/master.key` sits next to `secrets.enc`, so one
  backup, cloud sync or zip of the folder leaks both. Set `MCB_MASTER_KEY_FILE` to, for example,
  `~/.config/mc-bridge/master.key` (Windows: a file under `%APPDATA%` restricted with
  `icacls <file> /inheritance:r /grant:r %USERNAME%:F`; the Bridge cannot check Windows permissions).
  `mc-bridge doctor` warns while they share a folder.
- Passwords, PINs and TOTP codes are used once for a broker login and never stored.

## Declining a pending confirmation

A ticket that waits in Pending confirmations can be confirmed or declined. **Decline** (dashboard, with an optional short
reason, or `POST /v1/tickets/{ticketId}/reject` with an admin key from this computer, body empty or
`{"reason": "Wrong quantity"}`, 200 characters at most) ends the ticket at once, on the server:

- Only an **open** ticket can be declined. Declining one that is already declined answers 200 with the same state.
  A ticket that was confirmed, already used to send its order, or has expired answers **409** with
  `state: "confirmed" | "consumed" | "expired"`; an id the Bridge does not know answers 404.
- A declined ticket can never yield a confirmation code, whichever request comes second: confirming it afterwards is a
  409 with `state: "rejected"`, and declining a ticket someone just confirmed is a 409 with `state: "confirmed"`.
- It leaves `GET /v1/tickets`. The last ones declined stay readable for 15 minutes in memory
  (`GET /v1/tickets?state=rejected`; the dashboard shows them as "Recently declined") and are forgotten on restart.
- It is in the audit log as `ticket.rejected` (ticket id, account, symbol, side, mode, who declined, the reason you gave;
  never a code or key), and announced as the `ticket.rejected` event. An AI assistant that checks the ticket sees
  `status: "rejected"` and the reason ([mcp.md](mcp.md)); a webhook signal that was waiting on it ends as `rejected`
  (code `TICKET_REJECTED`).
- The same rules as confirming apply: admin key, this computer, and never an AI assistant, webhook or other automation.

## Audit log

Every key change, login, order step, confirmation or decline, kill-switch action and webhook signal is appended to
`data/audit/YYYY-MM-DD.jsonl` (IST days), redacted and hash-chained. `GET /v1/audit` (admin, this computer) queries it;
`GET /v1/audit/verify` checks the chain.

## Logs

One JSON line per event on stderr. Secret field names, Bridge keys, bearer tokens, JWTs and every decrypted credential
are masked; request bodies are never logged; webhook paths are logged without their tokens.

---

<!-- docs/guides/compliance.md -->

# Compliance notes

**Not legal advice.** These notes record how we read the rules that shape the Bridge's design, as of October 2026.
Anything marked **needs verification** must be checked against the primary SEBI, NSE and BSE circulars and each
broker's current notices before you rely on it. The detailed table, with circular numbers, is in
[ARCHITECTURE.md §12](../ARCHITECTURE.md#12-compliance-notes).

## What the Bridge is

Self-hosted, personal software. You run it on your own computer, with your own broker accounts and API keys, for
yourself and the family members SEBI allows. It ships no strategies or signals and hosts nothing for anyone else.

## SEBI retail algo framework

- SEBI's circular SEBI/HO/MIRSD/MIRSD-PoD/P/CIR/2025/0000013 of 4 February 2025 on safer participation of retail
  investors in algorithmic trading, and NSE's implementation standards NSE/INVG/67858 of 5 May 2025. Fully mandatory
  from 1 April 2026 after extensions (SEBI/HO/MIRSD/MIRSD-PoD/P/CIR/2025/108 and /132) (**needs verification**: the
  effective date and any changes after it).
- **Order threshold:** algos not registered with the exchange must stay at or below 10 orders per second per exchange
  segment, measured by the broker; brokers may set lower limits and may count modifications and cancellations
  (**needs verification per broker**). The Bridge's default cap is 5 per second per account, counting every order
  action, and the config cannot exceed 10.
- **Algo IDs:** the broker tags API orders (a generic tag below the threshold). The Bridge never invents tags.
- **Static IP:** API orders must come from a static IP registered with the broker (a primary and an optional
  secondary, changeable only occasionally); data and portfolio calls generally work from any IP (**needs
  verification** against CIR/2025/0000013, NSE/INVG/67858 and your broker's rules). Set `live.registeredIp` (and an optional `live.backupIp`) per account so the Bridge can warn before an order;
  the readiness check compares them with this computer's address when you turn its lookup on. A tunnel to a PC with
  a changing IP cannot place live orders. Ways to get a fixed address: [deployment.md](deployment.md).
- **Daily logout:** API sessions must end before the next trading day (**needs verification** per broker and against
  CIR/2025/0000013). The Bridge follows each broker's expiry, never
  stores TOTP secrets and never automates 2FA.
- **Order types:** plain market and some other order types may be restricted for API orders. The Bridge protects
  market orders by default or refuses them.

## Who may use it

A retail algo may be used by the client, spouse, dependent children and dependent parents (**needs verification**:
the family definition in CIR/2025/0000013 and NSE/INVG/67858). Running the Bridge for
anyone else, hosting it, or selling signals or strategies would likely make the operator an exchange-empanelled algo
provider, and black-box strategies may need Research Analyst registration (**legal review before any hosted
use**).

## Market data

Broker API terms generally allow market data for the account holder's personal use only (for example Kite Connect).
By default the Bridge serves only you, on loopback, and has no multi-user mode. It spreads reads across accounts
(pooling) only when you have accepted a versioned notice for them, they share one `holder` in your config (a family
member is a different user), the calling key may use them, and the broker's policy entry does not say `not-allowed`.
The notice says that no broker's published terms clearly allow pooling and none clearly forbids it, and that you are
responsible for your brokers' terms; every broker's entry is `unknown` today, so pooling also needs
`poolingWhenTermsUnknown` on the account (**needs verification per broker**; a legal read is recommended before turning
it on). Orders are never pooled.

### Other data sources

The Bridge can read from optional free sources and plugins you switch on. Each states the vendor's terms and shows them
before you turn it on; an unofficial or terms-sensitive source needs you to acknowledge a versioned notice first. Their
data is labelled `delayed` or `eod`, with an `official` flag and a confidence, and is never used for orders, risk checks,
paper fills or alerts. Free sources are for your own cross-checks and history, not a replacement for a licensed feed.
The Bridge does not redistribute any of it, and you must not pass it on. Anyone who builds something for other people on
top of this data should get a legal read on exchange data rules first. A plugin is code you run on your computer: the
Bridge limits what it can reach, but you decide whether to trust it ([sources.md](sources.md)).

### Tunnels and public endpoints

The Bridge itself never opens a public data endpoint, but **you can**. The Google Sheets route
([integrations/google-sheets/README.md](../../integrations/google-sheets/README.md), [excel-sheets.md](excel-sheets.md))
needs a tunnel so Google's servers can fetch prices. Point it at the optional **Sheets listener**
(`server.sheetsIngress`, set up by `mc-bridge expose sheets`, [expose-alerts.md](expose-alerts.md)), which serves only
`GET /xl/*` for read-only keys; never at the main API. Be clear about what that means:

- A tunnel **is a public endpoint**. Anyone who learns its URL and a read key can read what `/xl` serves (market data and
  read-only account views). On the main port a read key would reach far more, and can also engage the kill switch (it cannot
  cancel orders): that is why the separate listener exists.
- Your broker's market data then passes through a third party's servers (Google, and the tunnel provider). Broker data
  terms, such as Kite Connect's personal-use clause, may not allow redistribution to, or storage on, third-party
  servers, even for your own sheet (**needs verification per broker**). You carry that risk; if your broker's terms
  do not clearly allow it, use Excel on this computer instead (`/xl/*` over `127.0.0.1`), which needs no tunnel.
- The opt-in public ingress listener for webhooks (`server.publicIngress`) is different: it serves only `/hooks/*`,
  carries no market data out, and is not affected by this note.
- Never share the sheet or the tunnel URL with anyone else: serving data to other people is outside personal use.

## AI assistants

No regulator or broker guidance covers AI agents placing orders. An order an AI places through your key is still your
API order. The Bridge therefore keeps AI read-only by default, requires a person to confirm every AI-prepared order on
this computer, and logs which client prepared it (**gray area**).

## Brokers

Live order paths are wired for Dhan, Zerodha and Upstox; only Dhan has been verified against a live account. The other
adapters are tested against fixtures from each broker's documentation. Rate-limit figures carry a source URL and a
`verified` flag in the policy table.

<!-- docs/api/errors.md -->

# Error codes

Every error is `application/problem+json` with `code`, `status`, `detail`, `retryable` and `requestId`. The `code` is stable (codes are added, never renamed); `detail` is for people. `retryable` answers one question: is it safe to send exactly this request again? A write whose outcome is unknown is never retryable: check the order book first.

Rate-limit refusals (429) also say whose limit was hit: `scope` (`client`, `upstream`, `queue`, `consumer-cap`), `retryAfterMs` and `limit`. Read those fields, not `detail`. See [rate-limits.md](../guides/rate-limits.md).

Generated from `server/bridge/core/errors.mjs`.

| Code | HTTP | Retryable | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `INVALID_JSON` | 400 | no | The request body is not valid JSON |
| `VALIDATION_FAILED` | 400 | no | The request is not valid |
| `UNAUTHENTICATED` | 401 | no | A valid API key is required |
| `ACCOUNT_FORBIDDEN` | 403 | no | This API key may not use this account |
| `CANNOT_TRADE` | 403 | no | This account cannot trade right now (trading readiness) |
| `DAILY_LIMIT_REACHED` | 403 | no | A daily safety limit has been reached |
| `HOST_NOT_ALLOWED` | 403 | no | Requests must be addressed to an allowed host name |
| `LOOPBACK_ONLY` | 403 | no | This action is only available from this computer |
| `MARKET_CLOSED` | 403 | no | The market is closed for this instrument |
| `ORDER_GATE_CLOSED` | 403 | no | The live order gate refused this order. No order was sent |
| `ORIGIN_NOT_ALLOWED` | 403 | no | This web page origin is not on the allowlist |
| `PAPER_ONLY` | 403 | no | Live trading is not enabled for this account |
| `SCOPE_REQUIRED` | 403 | no | This API key does not have the scope this action needs |
| `ACCOUNT_NOT_FOUND` | 404 | no | No account with this id |
| `NOT_FOUND` | 404 | no | Not found |
| `ORDER_NOT_FOUND` | 404 | no | No order with this id |
| `SYMBOL_NOT_FOUND` | 404 | no | The symbol could not be resolved |
| `METHOD_NOT_ALLOWED` | 405 | no | Method not allowed |
| `AMBIGUOUS_SYMBOL` | 409 | no | The symbol matches more than one instrument. Choose one of the candidates |
| `DUPLICATE_CLIENT_ORDER_ID` | 409 | no | This clientOrderId was already used |
| `IDEMPOTENCY_IN_PROGRESS` | 409 | yes | A request with this idempotency key is still running |
| `IDEMPOTENCY_KEY_REUSED` | 409 | no | This idempotency key was already used with different parameters |
| `STATE_CONFLICT` | 409 | yes | The item changed or is busy; read it again |
| `PAYLOAD_TOO_LARGE` | 413 | no | The request body is too large |
| `UNSUPPORTED_MEDIA_TYPE` | 415 | no | Send the body as application/json |
| `CAPABILITY_UNSUPPORTED` | 422 | no | This broker does not support this request |
| `CONFIRMATION_REQUIRED` | 422 | no | This order needs a human confirmation first |
| `INVALID_ORDER` | 422 | no | The order failed a pre-trade check |
| `SESSION_EXPIRED` | 422 | no | The broker session has expired. Log in again |
| `KILL_SWITCH_ACTIVE` | 423 | no | The kill switch is on. No orders are being sent |
| `ORDER_RATE_LIMITED` | 429 | yes | Order rate cap for this account reached |
| `RATE_LIMITED` | 429 | yes | Too many requests from this API key |
| `SUBSCRIPTION_LIMIT` | 429 | no | The broker feed subscription limit was reached |
| `UPSTREAM_RATE_LIMITED` | 429 | yes | The broker's rate limit was reached |
| `INTERNAL` | 500 | no | Internal error |
| `NOT_IMPLEMENTED` | 501 | no | This part of the Bridge is not built yet |
| `UPSTREAM_ERROR` | 502 | no | The broker returned an error |
| `BROKER_UNAVAILABLE` | 503 | yes | The broker is not reachable right now |
| `POSITION_UNKNOWN` | 503 | yes | The current position could not be read, so nothing was placed |
| `OUTCOME_UNKNOWN` | 504 | no | The order outcome is unknown. Check the order book before sending it again |
| `UPSTREAM_TIMEOUT` | 504 | yes | The broker did not respond in time |
